studies.title: The Most Beautiful Of Tellings
studies.meaning: Three ayat stand before the story begins. The first points to the Book as clear. The second says it was sent in Arabic so its hearers could reason. The third promises the finest of narrations. Early scholars read that phrase in two ways. Either the telling itself is the most beautiful, or what is told is. Either way the last clause disarms, since the one receiving this knew nothing of it beforehand.
studies.historicalContext: Surah Yusuf belongs to the late Meccan years. By then the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) had lost the protection of close family, and the community faced steady pressure. Classical sources keep a report that people asked how the family of Jacob came to Egypt, and that the surah answered. Early scholars record that report, but they do not all agree on it. The general setting is not in doubt. A small, harassed group heard a long story about a favoured son thrown away and at last raised up.

keyTerms.note: The form works in two directions at once: something plainly evident in itself, and something that makes other things plain. Both senses are read here, so the Book is both lucid and clarifying.
The noun covers both the act of narrating and the thing narrated, and it comes from a root meaning to follow a trail. A story, in this idiom, is something tracked step by step.
Not ignorance as a fault but the ordinary state of someone who has simply not been told. The same word returns later in the story, describing brothers careless of a boy in their charge.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mecca ran on stories. Poets and reciters held audiences at markets and seasonal fairs, and a long narrative told well was the entertainment of a town with no books in circulation. Merchants brought tales along with goods from Syria and Yemen. To announce the finest of narrations to that audience was to enter a competition they knew how to judge, and to be judged by ears trained on it.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase rendered the finest of narrations occurs exactly once in the Quran, here. Its root returns at the surah's closing ayah, where the plural of the same word appears, so the whole of surah 12 is framed between two uses of one term. No other surah is given over to a single continuous story in this way.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Revelation is shown as news the one receiving it could not have had. The claim is not that the story improves you but that it is accurate. The ayah stakes the Book's standing on a story its first hearers could weigh against what they had heard elsewhere. Naming the language matters too. Being understood is treated as the point of sending a message, not an extra for the learned.

crossReferences.why: Closes the surah by returning to the same word for narrative and calling it guidance rather than invention.
States the same principle about language: every messenger was sent speaking the tongue of his people.
Repeats that the revelation was sent down as an Arabic recitation so that people might become mindful.

studies.applyIt: Read the whole surah in one sitting this week, start to finish, without stopping to look anything up. It runs about twenty minutes aloud. The opening promises a story that works as a story, and that claim is testable only at full length. Notice the first place where you want to know what happens next.
studies.explainEasier: God says this book is clear. He sent it in Arabic so that people could understand it. Now he will tell the Prophet the best story of all. It is a story the Prophet did not know before.

studies.title: Eleven Stars And A Dream
studies.meaning: The story opens with a child telling his father something he does not understand. Eleven stars, the sun and the moon, bowing down to him. The plural form used for them is the one Arabic reserves for rational beings, which early scholars note. Nothing is interpreted here. The dream is simply stated. The surah then takes a lifetime to fulfil it, so the reader holds the ending from the fourth verse onwards while the characters do not.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Early scholars link it to a period of sustained difficulty. The Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) had lost the protection of close family, and the message was making little progress. The surah tells one continuous story, which is unusual. Classical sources read it as given to a man whose situation looked far more like its opening than its ending.

keyTerms.note: A word for a bright heavenly body, distinct from the general term for stars. The number given is precise, eleven, which is why the dream is readable as a message rather than merely impressive.
An affectionate form of address, softer than the plain word for father. It recurs throughout this surah in the mouths of sons speaking to fathers, and it sets the register of the opening scene.

The plural form used for rational beings rather than for objects, applied here to stars. Arabic grammar marks the difference, so the dream already presents the heavenly bodies as standing in for people.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Dreams were taken seriously as information. Households discussed them in the morning. Men with a reputation for reading them were consulted before journeys and marriages. A dream of this kind, with a countable number and a clear gesture, would have been understood at once by everyone in the tent as a claim about rank. That is exactly why the father tells him to keep it to himself.
studies.didYouKnow: The surah is the only one in the Quran to tell a single continuous story from beginning to end. It calls itself the most beautiful of narrations in its third verse. This dream is the first event in it. The phrase used for the interpretation of such things returns at the story's close, in Joseph's own prayer.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The story begins with an ending that nobody inside it can see. That structure carries a claim. What is promised is real from the start, while the road to it runs through a pit, a prison and a famine. None of those look like the promise being kept. The dream is also given to a child, before any merit has been shown. That puts the promise before the qualification rather than after it.

crossReferences.why: Continues immediately, with the father telling him not to relate the dream to his brothers.
Shows the dream fulfilled at the end of the surah, with the family bowing before him.
Shows another prophet's dream taken as a matter to act on, between a father and a son.

studies.applyIt: Think of something you were sure about when you were young and later stopped mentioning because of how it was received. You do not have to act on it. Just take it out and look at it once, without the embarrassment. The surah opens by taking a child's account of a dream entirely seriously.
studies.explainEasier: Joseph was a boy when he told his father about a dream. He had seen eleven stars, the sun and the moon bowing down to him. The whole story that follows is about how that dream came true.

studies.title: Do Not Tell Your Brothers
studies.meaning: The first words Jacob speaks in this surah are a warning, not a celebration. He has heard something remarkable. His first instinct is to keep his son from being envied for it. He does not say the brothers will certainly plot. He says that telling them would give plotting somewhere to begin. The last clause moves the blame one step further back. It names an enemy who works through resentment rather than naming the brothers.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah came while the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) faced hostility from inside his own wider family. That is the situation this scene matches most closely. Early scholars report no particular occasion for this ayah. They do note that Jacob is shown from the start as a father who reads people well. That prepares a reader to trust his later judgements about his sons.

keyTerms.note: The word is for sleeping vision specifically, distinct from waking sight. The tradition treats a true dream as a small share of prophecy, which is why Jacob takes a boy's night vision seriously enough to act on it.

Hidden scheming rather than open hostility. The word and its relatives run through this surah nine times. They mark each turn where someone works indirectly, including a moment where devising is ascribed to God.
The adjective is the one used of the Book at the surah's opening: plainly evident. The enmity is not hidden, which makes falling for it a lapse of attention rather than a lack of information.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Dreams were public property in Arabia. A striking one was carried to an elder or a diviner and talked over. Reputations rose and fell on what a person was said to have seen at night. In that household the sons competed for their father's favour and for what he would leave behind. A dream that set one brother above the rest was not a private matter at all.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for scheming appears twice in this one ayah. It comes as a verb followed by a noun from the same root. Arabic uses that pairing for force, and English can only get near it with plot a plot. Across the whole Quran, that root falls nine times in surah 12. No other surah uses it as often.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Being a prophet does not spare a family from ordinary jealousy, and the surah says so by its fifth ayah. Jacob is given insight and still cannot stop what follows. Seeing ahead and being able to act are kept clearly apart. Naming a sworn enemy also places evil exactly. What happens to Joseph will be done by human hands and freely chosen. There is a prompting behind it, and the brothers still answer for taking it up.

crossReferences.why: Joseph names the same enemy at the reunion, closing the frame this early warning opens.
Gives the response to such a prompting: turn to God for refuge rather than argue with it.
Repeats that this enemy is an enemy, and says plainly what he is calling his followers towards.

studies.applyIt: There is something going well for you that you have been waiting to mention. Sit on it for a week. Not out of superstition, and not because the people around you are malicious, but because good news lands differently on someone in the middle of a hard stretch. Choose who hears it first with that in mind.
studies.explainEasier: Joseph tells his father about a dream he had. His father warns him not to tell his brothers, in case they plan something bad against him. He says that Satan is an open enemy to people.

studies.title: The Unravelling Of Accounts
studies.meaning: The phrase rendered interpretation of events means, word for word, the unravelling of accounts. Early scholars read it broadly. It covers dreams, but also the outcome of affairs and how a matter finally turns out. Jacob answers a dream with a promise that reaches three generations back. That puts his son inside an inheritance rather than a private fate. The second ayah steps outside the scene to address the listener. In this household there are signs for anyone who asks.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, in a surah spoken to a community that could not yet see how its own trouble would end. Naming Abraham and Isaac was pointed. The Meccan audience traced its own descent to Abraham and honoured him, so the line of favour described here was one they claimed. No particular occasion is reported for these ayat. What early scholars stress is that Joseph is placed inside a family already promised completion.

keyTerms.note: From a root meaning to gather up and collect for oneself. The image is not of a prize handed out but of something drawn together and kept close. That is why the tradition reads being chosen here as nearness rather than rank.
The second word means reports or things told, so the skill promised is wider than dream reading. It covers seeing what a sequence of events is finally heading towards, before it arrives.
An active participle: not for people who happen to hear, but for people who put a question. The ayah makes its own lessons depend on a reader willing to ask.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabs kept family lines the way other peoples keep land records. A man's standing was his line, said aloud and learned by heart for many generations. Any claim to inherit ran through it. A blessing completed on your grandfather and your great-grandfather would be completed on you. Being told that handed you a place in a chain everyone present could name. Joseph is given a line of descent before he is given anything else.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase for interpretation of events occurs eight times in surah 12, and it marks the arc of the whole story. It is promised here and repeated when Joseph is settled in Egypt. The prisoners use it, and so does the king's court. Joseph speaks it twice at the end. No other surah uses the term more than twice.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Being chosen is described as a gift with a lesson plan attached. To be chosen here means to be taught, which keeps favour from collapsing into mere status. The passage also pairs the naming of God as Knowing and Wise with a promise about the future. A reader is told in advance that the wreckage of the next thirty ayat is not a breakdown of the plan. Signs are said to lie in the story for those who ask.

crossReferences.why: Joseph repeats this promise back to God as thanks, once it has finally been fulfilled.
Shows Jacob passing the same inherited commitment on to his own sons as he dies.
Lists this line, Abraham through Isaac and Jacob to Joseph, as one guided sequence.

studies.applyIt: Pick one good thing you inherited rather than earned: a habit of prayer kept in the house, an uncle who kept turning up, a language you were given. Say where it came from, out loud, to someone younger than you. This passage hands Joseph a chain before it hands him anything he has worked for.
studies.explainEasier: Jacob tells Joseph that God will pick him out. God will teach him what dreams and events really mean. He will finish his gift to Joseph and his family, just as he did for Abraham and Isaac.

studies.title: Afterwards You Will Be Decent
studies.meaning: The brothers build a case before they build a plan. They state their grievance as arithmetic: two sons against a whole band. It ends by finding their father in the wrong rather than admitting envy. Then comes the chilling last clause. Once this is done, they say, you will be decent people. Early scholars note that they book their repentance in advance. That is what makes the sentence worse than the murder plan before it.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The people who heard this surah were watching relatives turn against relatives over the new message. Kinship should have kept them safe, and it did not. No occasion is reported for these two ayat. Classical commentary sets the scene inside a large household of half-brothers. It reads the phrase about a whole band as the talk of a working group of grown men who saw themselves as the household's real strength.

keyTerms.note: A word for men bound tightly enough to act as one, with a sense of numbers that can get things done. The brothers use it as their argument: usefulness ought to earn affection.
The idiom means his attention and favour turned towards you. Removing a rival is described as clearing a face, which makes love sound like a space with room for only one.

The standard Quranic word for those whose deeds are sound. Placing it after a planned crime is deliberate, and early scholars read the brothers as meaning real repentance later rather than mocking the idea.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Households in that world were labour units. Sons pastured the flocks, watered them, moved camp, defended the herd at night, and a father's regard tended to follow the work. Being many mattered: raiding parties counted heads before they chose a target, and a family with grown sons was left alone. The brothers are arguing from a real economy, which is exactly why they cannot see what their father sees.
studies.didYouKnow: Not one of Joseph's brothers is named anywhere in the Quran. Later Israelite tradition calls the youngest Benjamin, but the surah calls him only his brother. The eldest speaks at a decisive moment and is named only as their eldest. In a story this detailed, leaving them unnamed stands out. It keeps the attention on what people do rather than on who they are.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage catches one particular self-deception. The brothers treat repentance as a cost they have already set aside. Mercy is real, and they do receive it in the end, but only after ruin, not as the discount they assumed. The ayat also show wrongdoing arriving dressed as fairness. Nothing they say is untrue about the facts. The twist is in what they decide a father owes them for being useful.

crossReferences.why: The brothers finally ask for forgiveness in earnest, decades after scheduling it here as an afterthought.
Distinguishes turning back soon after wrong from repentance deferred until the moment of loss.
The other Quranic account of a brother killed out of envy, told with the same refusal to excuse it.

studies.applyIt: Notice the next time you catch yourself thinking you will make something right later. That thought is doing work: it is buying permission for the thing you are about to do. Try naming it aloud when it arrives, in plain words, without deciding anything else. Most people find the plan does not survive being said.
studies.explainEasier: The brothers say their father loves Joseph and his little brother more than them. So they make a plan. They will kill Joseph, or take him far away. Then their father will look at them instead.

studies.title: One Voice In The Council
studies.meaning: One voice inside the council brings the sentence down from death to abandonment. The story lets that count for something without calling it good. The plan is still to leave a boy at the bottom of a cistern on a caravan route and then to hope. Early scholars differ over who spoke. Most name the eldest or another of the older brothers, and the surah leaves him unnamed. His last words give the plan away entirely: if you are going to act at all.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Wells and cisterns along trade routes were shared property, kept up by whoever used them, and a body dropped into one was not necessarily found. Early scholars report no occasion for this ayah. They read the speaker's move as the first sign that the brothers are not a single mind, a crack that widens much later when one of them refuses to leave Egypt without the youngest.

keyTerms.gloss: the hidden depth of the well
keyTerms.note: The first word means the part where a thing is lost to sight. It is not simply the bottom but the place where seeing stops, which is what the brothers actually want.
A group defined by being in motion, from the verb to journey. The word carries no suggestion of trade or ownership, only of people passing through who will not be there tomorrow.
A verb used of discarding as much as of placing. The same root will describe the shirt laid over an old man's face at the end of the surah, in a gesture that reverses this one.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: An unused cistern beside a caravan track was an ordinary sight in the land between Syria and Egypt. Travellers stopped at known water. They sent a man down with a bucket, watered the animals, and moved on before the heat. Whatever was in the well when they arrived became theirs by finding it. The brothers are not gambling wildly. They are using a known feature of the road to make a boy someone else's property.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase for the hidden depth of the well occurs exactly twice in the Quran. It comes here, where the plan is proposed, and five ayat later, where it is carried out. The repetition is word for word. The plan and the doing of it are told in the same language, and nothing at all is added at the moment it happens.
studies.theologicalSignificance: A lesser wrong is still a wrong. The passage records the softening without softening the verdict. It is also the first place where the story's machinery shows. The brothers choose the well exactly because a caravan might take him, and that hope of theirs is the road by which Joseph reaches Egypt. What they mean as disposal turns out to be transport. What people intend and what results are shown running on separate tracks.

crossReferences.why: Repeats this proposal word for word as it is carried out, with a promise added to it.
The caravan the speaker hoped for does arrive, and lifts Joseph out towards Egypt.
States the pattern directly: they plan, and God plans, and God is the best of planners.

studies.applyIt: Think of a room where you were the one who softened something that was still wrong: the joke you toned down instead of stopping, the decision you made less bad. Give it its right name today, to yourself, without excusing the room or condemning yourself. Reducing harm is worth doing. It is not the same as refusing.
studies.explainEasier: One brother says they should not kill Joseph. Instead he tells them to drop him into the bottom of a well, where a passing group of travellers might find him and take him away.

studies.title: Why Do You Not Trust Us
studies.meaning: Two ayat of pure persuasion, and every move in them is recognisable. They open with a reproach dressed as a question, which puts their father on the defensive before any request is made. They offer a reason a child would want: roaming and play. They close with a guarantee. Early scholars note that the word they use for keeping him safe is the one their father will later apply to God alone.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The audience knew the shape of this conversation, since agreements in that society were made face to face and secured by the standing of the speaker rather than by writing. No occasion is reported for these ayat. Early scholars observe that the brothers make no threat and tell no outright lie here. The deception is entirely in what they leave out, which is what makes the exchange hard to refuse.

keyTerms.note: From the root that gives the words for safety and for faith itself. To trust someone with a person is, in this vocabulary, to place them where no harm can reach, which is the claim being made.
The root means to be pure and unmixed, as honey is unmixed, and then to give counsel with nothing hidden in it. They choose the one word that most directly contradicts what they are doing.
A participle for someone actively preserving a thing from loss. It is the vocabulary of a shepherd with a flock, and their father will take the same word away from them later.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Boys went out with the flocks as soon as they could keep up. Grazing meant a full day away from camp, sometimes further. The older sons carried real responsibility for whoever went with them. Play was part of it: wrestling, footraces, throwing at marks. Herding families everywhere have passed long hours that way. Nothing in the request would have sounded odd to anyone listening. That is exactly the difficulty.
studies.didYouKnow: The brothers ask why their father does not trust them. Their verb carries an unusual reading mark in the standard written text. A small sign above the letter points to a sound that reciters handle in more than one way. It is one of the few places where the writing keeps a sound that ordinary spelling cannot show.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage shows how agreement gets manufactured. Jacob is not overpowered. He is talked round by people using the words of care, and the Quran holds them fully to account for that. It also sets up one of the surah's quiet arguments. The promises people give each other are worth exactly what the people are worth. That is why the same word for keeping safe is later taken from human hands and given to God.

crossReferences.why: Jacob answers a nearly identical request years later by transferring the word guardian to God.
The brothers repeat this same guarantee about the youngest, in almost the same words.
Asks for verification when news arrives, rather than acting on an account nobody has checked.

studies.applyIt: Listen for the shape of the request next time someone asks you for something: a small reproach first, then a reason you would like to be true, then a promise at the end. That order is not proof of bad faith. It is worth noticing anyway. When you hear it, ask one plain question about the part nobody has mentioned.
studies.explainEasier: The brothers ask their father why he will not trust them with Joseph. They say they only want good for him. They ask to take him out the next day to run about and play, and they promise to look after him.

studies.title: The Wolf And The Grief
studies.meaning: Jacob gives two reasons and they are not the same kind. The first is grief at the separation itself, stated as something that happens to him rather than as an argument. The second is a fear he can name: a wolf, and inattention. The brothers seize the second and ignore the first, answering the risk while stepping over the sorrow. In doing so they are handed the story they will tell, and they use it four ayat later.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Wolves were a live danger to flocks in Palestine and northern Arabia, not a figure of speech, and any listener with animals had lost one. No occasion is reported for these ayat. Read in the setting of the surah's first hearers, a father fearing to lose a son while others looked away carried an edge: the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) was addressing people whose own kin were failing to protect them.

keyTerms.note: The verb makes the grief the subject and Jacob its object, so sorrow is something done to him rather than something he produces. Arabic can put a feeling in the active voice this way; English usually cannot.
Definite, as though a particular known animal. Flocks in that country lost sheep to wolves every season, so the article is the one a shepherd uses for a familiar and recurring threat.
The same word the surah's opening used of a listener who had simply not been told. Here it names a lapse with consequences, and Jacob places the real danger in it rather than in the animal.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Guarding a flock at night meant staying awake in shifts within earshot of the animals. A wolf takes what is at the edge, and what is at the edge is whatever the guard has stopped watching. Shepherds knew this exactly, and the accusation folded into the word careless would have stung. Jacob is not warning about an animal. He is telling grown sons that the danger enters through their attention.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for wolf occurs three times in the entire Quran, all of them in surah 12 and all within five ayat: twice here, and once when the brothers report the death. It appears nowhere else in the Book. The animal exists in the Quran only as the thing Jacob feared and the thing his sons used as cover.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Prophets are shown grieving in ordinary ways, and the Quran does not treat that as a flaw. Jacob's sorrow is reported before his reasoning. That places feeling inside faith rather than beneath it. The passage also makes a point about knowing ahead. He senses what is coming and is not given the power to stop it. Knowing and controlling belong to different hands, and the surah keeps them apart from the start.

crossReferences.why: The brothers return with exactly the excuse their father has just put into their mouths.
Shows where this grief finally goes: eyes whitened with sorrow, and no complaint made to people.
Jacob names the only place he takes his sorrow, and it is not to his sons.

studies.applyIt: Say the harder half of your reason out loud this week. Most people give the reason that can be argued with and keep the real one to themselves: not the risk, but that they will miss someone, or feel left out, or be afraid. Give both, in that order, to one person. Watch which half they answer.
studies.explainEasier: Jacob tells his sons it makes him sad to see Joseph go. He is afraid a wolf will eat him while they are not looking. They say that could never happen, since there are so many of them.

studies.title: Inspired At The Bottom
studies.meaning: The worst moment of the story is told in half a sentence, and then the account turns away from the brothers. God speaks to the boy in the well, and what He says is not comfort but a fact about the future: you will tell them of this, and they will not know you. The tense matters, since the outcome is settled while Joseph is still down there. The next ayah cuts to the brothers arriving at nightfall, weeping.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, from the years when the community had least reason to expect relief. They were being given accounts of prophets whose situations turned right round. No occasion is reported for these ayat. Early scholars note that the inspiration here is not counted as the start of prophethood. They differ over whether Joseph was a boy receiving a message or already held the office. The surah does not settle it.

keyTerms.note: The verb means to gather a thing into one, and applied to a decision it means to make the intention whole and final. Not a drift into wrongdoing but a settled resolve taken as a group.
The root covers any swift, hidden communication. It is used of prophets, but also of bees and of a mother's heart, so its presence does not by itself settle what office Joseph held.
The hour after sunset when a camp gathers and the day's account is given. Naming it places the brothers' arrival at the exact moment a missing person is noticed by everyone at once.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Evening was when a camp came back together. Animals came in and fires were lit. Whoever was missing was missed at once, in front of everyone. Grief in that society was done aloud and in company. Weeping was a public act with its own rules, and a family that did not wail would have been talked about. Arriving at that hour, in tears, put the brothers inside a script their father could not easily break into.
studies.didYouKnow: The promise made in the well is kept seventy-four ayat later. Joseph asks his brothers whether they know what they did, and they still do not know him. The two moments turn on the same pair of ideas: telling, and not knowing. A sentence spoken into a cistern is answered in a palace.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Revelation reaches a person at the point where he can do nothing, and it does not take the situation away. Joseph stays in the well. He is simply told how it ends. That is one clear account of what God's help often looks like, and the surah shows it again later. The promise arrives long before the rescue. It also settles early that God is there in the pit, which changes how everything afterwards reads.

crossReferences.why: The moment the promise is kept: Joseph names the deed while they still do not know him.
Inspiration given to a mother as she loses a child, with his return promised in advance.
States as a general rule what this scene enacts, and states it twice over.

studies.applyIt: Think about what you would want to hear at the bottom of something, then notice that this passage does not offer comfort. It offers a fact. If you are in a long difficulty now, try writing one sentence describing how you will speak about it afterwards, in the past tense. Keep it somewhere you will find it later.
studies.explainEasier: The brothers take Joseph away and drop him into the well. While he is down there, God tells him that one day he will tell them what they did. Then they go home to their father, crying.

studies.title: Even Though We Are Truthful
studies.meaning: The lie is well built and it collapses at the last clause. They supply detail nobody can check: a race, belongings left at a mark, a wolf. Then they add a sentence no one asked for. You will not believe us, even if we are being truthful. Early scholars have long noticed the tell. Guilt expects disbelief and guards against it in advance, and the phrasing they choose spares them from ever stating plainly that they are honest.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Oral testimony was the whole of evidence in that world. A claim stood or fell on the standing of the person making it and on whether a group would back him, so several voices telling one account was ordinarily decisive. No occasion is reported for this ayah. Early scholars read what follows as showing Jacob unpersuaded, not by any counter-evidence but simply by knowing his sons.

keyTerms.note: A form that means competing to get ahead. The same verb describes Joseph and the governor's wife racing for the door much later, which is one of several verbal echoes binding the surah together.
Portable goods, the things a traveller carries and puts down. The word is used across the Quran for the enjoyments of this world, always with the suggestion of something set down and left behind.

The standard word for those whose speech matches reality. The brothers apply it to themselves inside a conditional, which is the weakest possible way to claim it, and the surah gives it to Joseph later in full.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Racing was the ordinary sport of young men, on foot and on horseback. It was the natural thing to do while animals grazed. Belongings piled at a mark were how a party kept camp while it played. Every detail the brothers name is unremarkable. That is exactly what makes the account believable. A false story that worked in a spoken culture had to be built out of things everyone had done.
studies.didYouKnow: The word the brothers claim for themselves here, truthful, comes back twice later in the surah. Both times it is given to Joseph. Once a witness in the household says it, after looking at a torn shirt. Once the woman who had accused him says it. The same word travels from the mouths of liars to a public verdict about the man they lied about.
studies.theologicalSignificance: A lie that works is still written down as a lie. The surah follows this one for seventy ayat, until the people who told it say so themselves. That is the Quran's usual way with deception. Not exposure at once, but exposure in the end, from the mouths of those who did it. The passage also shows how trust between people really works. Jacob answers the character behind the account rather than the account.

crossReferences.why: Jacob replies without contesting a single detail, naming instead what their own souls have done.
A torn shirt settles a later dispute the way a bloodied shirt failed to settle this one.
The brothers finally supply the verdict themselves, admitting under oath that they were wrong.

studies.applyIt: Notice, this week, the sentence you add at the end. The extra reassurance, the complaint that nobody will believe you anyway, the joke that lets you take it back. Say the plain thing and then stop talking. If the silence feels unfinished, that feeling is worth examining rather than filling.
studies.explainEasier: The brothers come home and tell their father that they were running a race and left Joseph with their things. They say a wolf ate him. Then they add that he will not believe them anyway.

studies.title: Patience Without Complaint
studies.meaning: The evidence is a shirt with blood on it, and the verse calls the blood false before the father says anything. He does not accuse anyone of a specific act. He says their own selves made something look attractive to them, which refuses the story while leaving the deed unnamed. Then two short phrases: a patience described as beautiful, and God named as the one whose help is sought against what they describe. He answers the account rather than the sons.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah was revealed to a community under pressure, and to a man whose own kin had turned against him. Early scholars note the resemblance without pressing it. The scene itself belongs to the world of the patriarchs. A family with flocks, several sons by different mothers, and an inheritance of standing that made visible favour a dangerous thing.

keyTerms.note: A verb for dressing something up so that it looks desirable. It places responsibility inside the sons without naming what they did, which is how the father refuses the story without charging them with a crime.

The adjective means beautiful in the ordinary aesthetic sense. Early scholars explain the phrase as patience with no complaint attached, and it appears twice in this surah, both times from the same speaker.

keyTerms.gloss: the One whose help is sought
keyTerms.note: A passive participle naming God by what is done towards Him, the one appealed to. It is a rare form, and it turns the sentence into an appeal without raising the voice at anybody.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A torn or bloodied garment was standard evidence in a world without documents. Claims about a death were backed by whatever could be carried home. An animal attack was a likely loss for a family grazing flocks at a distance. The father's rejection of the story rests on a detail the early scholars supply. The shirt came back bloodied but not torn.
studies.didYouKnow: The shirt appears three times in this surah and each time it changes the situation. It is bloodied here as false evidence. Later it is torn from behind as proof of innocence. Finally it is cast over a blind father's face to restore his sight. Classical scholars trace the garment through the story as one of its threads.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Patience is qualified rather than commanded. That is the distinctive move. Adding the word beautiful separates endurance from resignation, and from the public show of grief. The surah later shows the same man weeping until he loses his sight. So the beauty is not composure. Naming God as the one whose help is sought against a description keeps the appeal aimed at the falsehood rather than at people.

crossReferences.why: Repeats the same phrase years later, when a second son is lost.
Shows where the complaint does go, addressed to God rather than to the sons.
Uses the same adjective for patience in a command given to the Prophet.

studies.applyIt: Next time you are wronged and want to say so, try separating the two things this verse separates: refusing the false account, and going after the person who gave it. Say the first out loud and leave the second unsaid. Notice how much of the urge to speak was actually about the second.
studies.explainEasier: The brothers brought their father a shirt with fake blood on it. He did not believe them. He said he would wait with patience and no complaining, and that God would help him.

studies.title: Sold For A Few Coins
studies.meaning: Two ayat move Joseph from a well to a market. The water-carrier's shout is delight at a windfall. The caravan's next act is to hide him as merchandise, which shows the sale was not above board from the start. Then he is sold cheap. Early scholars differ over who the sellers were, the caravan or the brothers coming back, and over the worth of the coins. Both readings agree the price was contemptible and that the sellers wanted him gone.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, spoken to a trading city. Mecca lived on caravans between Yemen and Syria, and it knew the trade in people that moved alongside goods. No occasion is reported for these ayat. Early scholars dwell on the phrase about God being aware of what they did. They read it as the story refusing to let a quiet sale on a trade road pass without a witness.

keyTerms.note: From the root for glad tidings, and also for the skin, since good news shows in the face. The cry is one of pure profit, and the same root names the messenger who later restores an old man's sight.
Stock carried for sale, a portion cut off from a larger holding. The brothers will come to Egypt years later carrying poor goods described with this very word, asking for charity.

The root later gave the word for giving the world up, treating a thing as beneath wanting. Applied to sellers of a person it becomes damning. They did not price the sale too low; they priced him too low.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Caravans ran on thin margins and quick decisions. A party watering at a well would send one man down with a bucket while the rest held the animals, and anything gained on the road was divided by custom among those present. Slaves moved along the same routes as incense and hides, sold at the next town by men who had no interest in a story. Concealment kept a find off the accounting.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for silver coins occurs exactly once in the whole Quran, in this ayah. The Book rarely names a currency in a sale. Usually it speaks only of a small price. Here the sum named is the price paid for a prophet, by people who wanted rid of him.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Putting a price on something is shown as a human act, not a fact about the thing priced. The market prices Joseph at a few coins. On the same day God is described as fully aware of the sale. The surah lets the two judgements sit side by side without comment. It also starts a pattern the story will repeat. Every step taken to bring Joseph down moves him closer to where he ends up.

crossReferences.why: The buyer in Egypt immediately reverses the valuation, telling his household to treat him honourably.
The brothers arrive years later with scant goods, the same word used for Joseph when hidden.
Names the deeper version of this trade: exchanging a covenant with God for a small price.

studies.applyIt: Find one thing today that you priced too low: an hour, a skill, a person's time you took for granted, or your own. Say what a fair figure would have been. You do not need to fix it or tell anyone. The point is to notice that a price is something people decide, and that deciding badly leaves a trace.
studies.explainEasier: A group of travellers stops at the well. The man sent for water pulls up his bucket and finds a boy. They hide him and take him with them. Later they sell him for only a few coins.

studies.title: Established In The Land
studies.meaning: A slave is bought, and the buyer tells his wife to treat him well. He hopes the boy will prove useful or become a son. The narrative then steps outside the scene to say what was actually happening. This was establishment, and its purpose was teaching. Early scholars note that the two clauses do not match in scale. A household instruction in one Egyptian house is reported as the means by which God settled a young man exactly where he needed to be.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The story is set in Egypt, and the surah gives its officials titles rather than names, which the classical sources read as deliberate. Joseph has just been sold by a passing caravan for a low price. Early scholars place the episode inside a long-standing slave trade running between the Levant and Egypt, along the same routes the Meccan audience used for their own commerce.

keyTerms.note: A verb for making a place firm for someone, from a root for location and capacity. It is used later in the surah of his rise to authority, so one word covers a household and a kingdom.
The phrase covers the reading of dreams and of events, since the word for interpretation means tracing something back to its origin. It returns at the end of the surah in his closing prayer.
An active participle for the one who comes out on top of something. Applied to God over His own affair it says the outcome is not in question, while the next clause says most people cannot see that.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Household slavery in the ancient Near East varied widely. It ranged from brutal labour to posts of real trust. A capable young man could end up managing an estate's accounts. Adoption was a recognised way for a childless couple to secure their property and their old age. The instruction to treat him well was an investment decision as much as a kindness. Everybody hearing it understood that.
studies.didYouKnow: The surah names almost nobody. Joseph is named, and Jacob, and the country; the man who buys him, his wife, the king and the officials all appear by title or description alone. Classical scholars note the pattern, and it keeps the attention on what happens rather than on who exactly did it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Providence is described as working through motives that have nothing to do with it. The buyer wants a useful servant or an heir. What actually occurs is placement and instruction. The passage states both levels without suggesting the human motive was false. That is the point. God's control over His affair does not require the people inside it to know they are. The final clause is about that ignorance.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same word for establishment when he later holds authority in the land.
Has Joseph name this whole sequence as good that God did to him.
Shows a parallel household decision in Egypt, sparing another child for use.

studies.applyIt: Look back at one arrangement you did not choose: a placement, a job taken because you needed the money, a move made for someone else's reasons. Ask what you learned there that you use now. The verse does not promise everything is for the best. It notices that instruction often arrives through doors somebody else opened.
studies.explainEasier: The man who bought Joseph in Egypt told his wife to look after him well. He thought Joseph might be useful, or might even become their son. God was placing Joseph where he needed to be.

studies.title: He Has Given Me A Home
studies.meaning: He reaches full growth, and with it judgement and knowledge, described as given rather than earned. Then the test. Joseph's refusal has three parts. He appeals to God, he gives a reason drawn from thanks, and he states a general truth about wrongdoers. The middle part is famously open, since the word for lord can mean the master of the house or God. Early scholars read it both ways, and several allow both at once. The argument holds either way: shelter is not paid back with betrayal.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The audience knew household slavery at close range. Mecca's own houses ran on it, and a servant's standing rested entirely on the family that held him. No occasion is reported for these ayat. Early scholars note that Joseph is at this point a young man with no kin in the country, no legal standing of his own, and nobody to appeal to. That is the situation the refusal is made from.

keyTerms.note: The point where growth is complete and a person is at their firmest. The Quran uses it for the age of responsibility rather than a fixed number, and early scholars give a range instead of a figure.
A form built for repeated, gradual effort, from a root about going back and forth in search of water or pasture. It describes persuasion applied over time rather than a single approach.
Not an exclamation but a declaration of shelter sought. Joseph's first move under pressure is to place himself somewhere, and the phrase is his answer rather than an argument against her.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A servant brought from outside had no tribe within reach, and tribe was the only insurance in that world. An accusation from the household he lived in could not be answered by producing relatives who would swear for him. The doors of a great house shut from the inside. Every listener understood that Joseph's refusal was made by someone with no protection at all, which is what gives the scene its weight.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase Joseph uses to take refuge occurs exactly twice in the Quran. Both times he is the one who says it. Once here, and once much later in Egypt, when he refuses to hold the wrong man. The same three syllables mark the two moments where he turns down something he could have done and got away with.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Integrity is grounded in gratitude rather than in rules. Joseph does not cite a prohibition; he names a kindness he has received and declines to answer it with harm, and the passage lets that stand as sufficient. The pairing of the two ayat also matters. Judgement and knowledge are given first, and the test follows immediately, so what God grants is shown being spent rather than displayed.

crossReferences.why: Joseph names the cost of this refusal and asks for help holding to it.
The only other place he takes refuge in this phrase, again refusing an easy injustice.
The scene is settled publicly years later, when she states in front of everyone that he resisted.

studies.applyIt: Think of a place where you are treated well and could take advantage without being caught. A house, a job, a friendship that runs on trust rather than on paperwork. Name it specifically today, and name what you would be repaying if you did. Gratitude is a more durable brake than fear of being found out.
studies.explainEasier: Joseph grows up, and God gives him good sense and knowledge. The woman of the house locks the doors and asks him to come to her. He says no. Her husband gave him a good home.

studies.title: The Proof Of His Lord
studies.meaning: This is the most carefully weighed ayah in the surah, and the sentence is left unfinished on purpose. She resolved, and he would have, had he not seen the proof of his Lord. Early scholars differ widely on the second verb. Some read a natural pull that never became intent. Some read a movement stopped before it formed. Some read the whole clause as governed by the exception that follows. All agree on the outcome and the verdict. Evil was turned aside from him, and he is named among God's chosen servants.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Reports about what the proof was circulated early and freely. Most of them were drawn from Israelite tradition rather than from any sound account. The major commentaries record them while leaving the question open. The surah itself says only that it came from his Lord. The setting is unchanged: a closed house, a locked door, and a young man with no standing in the country.

keyTerms.note: The verb covers everything from a passing stir in the chest to a settled resolve. Arabic leaves the strength unspecified, and that width is exactly why the classical readings of this ayah differ.
A demonstration that ends argument, used across the Quran for evidence that leaves nothing to answer. The word says the intervention was something shown to him, not a feeling that came over him.
A passive form: not those who purified themselves but those God purified and set apart. It occurs eight times in the Quran and is always about what has been done to a servant.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: In a great Egyptian house the inner rooms were the one place with no witnesses. A household servant knew every listener and every door. Arabia's own houses worked the same way. That is why oaths and testimony mattered so much there, and why a charge made behind closed doors was nearly impossible to answer. What protects Joseph here is not a lock or a bystander. It is something seen that nobody else in the room saw.
studies.didYouKnow: The exact wording of this ayah has been argued over since the earliest generations. Arabic marks no full stop, and where the pause falls changes the sense. Reciters differ over where to breathe in it. That choice is itself a reading. It is why the classical commentaries treat recitation and meaning together here.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Protection from wrongdoing is described as something God does, not merely something a person achieves. That is the point of the passive form at the end: Joseph is called one who was made pure. The ayah also refuses to flatter him. It concedes that he was a young man in a closed room and leaves the pull real, which makes his standing a matter of grace received rather than temperament.

crossReferences.why: Names the same pull directly, and says only mercy keeps a soul from where it leans.
The enemy concedes he has no power over servants whom God has made pure, using this same term.
States generally that without God's favour nobody among us would ever be purified.

studies.applyIt: Bring to mind the last time you did not do something you wanted to do. Notice that you probably credit yourself for it. Try, once today, thanking God for it instead, in one sentence, without false modesty. The change is small and it alters how you carry the next occasion, which is the point.
studies.explainEasier: The woman wanted Joseph, and he would have wanted her too. But God showed him a clear sign, and he turned away. God kept him safe from doing wrong. He was one of God's chosen servants.

studies.title: Caught At The Door
studies.meaning: Everything in this ayah is motion until it stops at a door. They race, the shirt tears, and the master of the house is standing there. Then the accusation arrives before anyone has asked a question. It is framed as a matter of sentencing rather than as a claim: what is the penalty for a man who intended harm to your wife. Early scholars note the move. By starting at the punishment she buries the guilt inside her own sentence.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The audience knew how quickly a charge could settle a matter when the accuser had standing and the accused had none. No occasion is reported for this ayah. Early scholars are careful to note that the surah names nobody here except Joseph. The man at the door is only her master, and she is only the one in whose house he lived, which keeps the scene focused on the conduct rather than the persons.

keyTerms.note: A form built for competing to arrive first, and the same root the brothers used when they claimed to have gone off racing. Both times Joseph is wronged, someone is running.
The classical lexicons distinguish this verb from a crosswise tear. It describes cloth split along its length, which is what happens when a garment is seized while its wearer is moving away.
The word for the head of a household, used here of her husband. The Quran leaves him without a name or an office at this point, and only later calls him by his title in the city.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A shirt was not one garment among many. Most people owned a single main outer piece, worn until it wore out. It was the thing you were known by at a distance. Cloth cost a lot, was mended again and again, and was passed on. So a torn shirt was evidence anyone could read. Everyone in the surah's first audience had spent a season wearing something that showed exactly how it got damaged.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb for racing one another appears in only two scenes of this surah. Both are moments when Joseph is falsely accused. The brothers claim they went off racing and left him behind. Here he and the woman race for a door. Elsewhere in the Quran the same root carries the command to race towards good.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage records how a false account gets its advantage. It is told first, told loudly, and told in the grammar of a verdict. That is a point about human judgement rather than about God, and the surah works it out slowly. Truth in this story is never saved by being obvious. It waits. In the end it is shown by evidence and by confession, and both take years to arrive.

crossReferences.why: A witness answers the accusation with physical reasoning instead of a competing assertion.
The same woman states the truth publicly once nothing further depends on the lie.
Requires witnesses to stand for fairness even when the testimony runs against their own household.

studies.applyIt: Notice the next time you hear a complaint that arrives already sentenced: not what happened, but what should be done about what happened. Slow down and ask for the first half. You are not doubting the person by asking. You are giving the account somewhere to be checked, which is what this scene never gets.
studies.explainEasier: They both ran for the door, and she tore his shirt from behind. Her husband was standing there. She said at once that Joseph had tried to harm her, and asked for him to be jailed or punished.

studies.title: The Evidence Of A Tear
studies.meaning: A witness offers a test rather than an opinion. If the shirt is torn at the front, she is truthful; if at the back, she is not. The reasoning is physical: a man pressing forward has his front seized, a man escaping has his back caught. Early scholars differ over who the witness was. Some report an infant made to speak, others a member of the household with the sense to see the point. The surah simply says a witness, and never identifies him.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Disputes in seventh-century Arabia were normally settled by oath and by backing testimony. A case decided by looking closely at an object struck the first hearers as unusual. No occasion is reported for these ayat. Early scholars dwell on the fact that the witness belongs to her own household. That removes any suspicion that he speaks for the outsider rather than for the evidence.

keyTerms.note: Indefinite, so the surah declines to identify him. The root means to be present and to see, and this witness testifies to a method of reading evidence rather than to anything he saw happen.
The plain word for a rear side. It also gives the verbs for turning away and for managing an affair from behind the scenes, both of which describe what is happening in this room.
The word the brothers had claimed for themselves under a conditional. Here it is given to Joseph as a conclusion drawn from cloth, and it is given to him again later by the woman herself.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Reading marks on the ground was an ordinary skill in that world. From prints a tracker could tell how many camels had passed, how heavily they were loaded, and how long ago. That skill settled disputes over theft and straying animals across the desert. The witness is doing what a good tracker does, applied to a garment. His argument would have struck the first audience as expert rather than clever.
studies.didYouKnow: The wording rendered a witness testified occurs only twice in the Quran. It comes here, and in a later surah where the witness is one of the Children of Israel. In both places the verb is followed at once by its own subject noun. Arabic uses that doubling to give the act of testifying a weight the sentence would not otherwise carry.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Truth is defended here by ordinary reasoning. No miracle is involved, even on the readings that make the witness an infant, since what he offers is an argument. The Quran again and again rests belief on evidence people can weigh, and this small scene in a house works the same way. It also shows innocence needing someone to speak for it. Being innocent did not clear Joseph. Someone speaking up did.

crossReferences.why: The evidence is accepted and then the matter is quietly buried rather than put right.
The confession that finally makes public what this shirt established privately years before.
Sets out how a serious accusation is to be weighed rather than repeated on its own strength.

studies.applyIt: The next time two people you know give you conflicting accounts, resist choosing by who you like more. Look for one checkable detail, however small, and check it. It will often decide nothing. Doing it anyway changes what you are, from someone who picks sides to someone who looks at the shirt.
studies.explainEasier: Joseph says she was the one who tried to make him come to her. Someone from her house says to look at his shirt. If it is torn at the back, then Joseph is telling the truth.

studies.title: Turn Away From This
studies.meaning: The verdict is reached and then withdrawn from public view. He sees the tear, names the scheme, and pronounces on it in a general sentence about schemes. Then comes the management: Joseph is told to let the matter drop, and she is told to seek forgiveness. Nobody is cleared, nobody is charged. Early scholars read the whole exchange as a household closing ranks, which is why Joseph's name stays under a cloud for years afterwards.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. A great house in that world was a small state, and its head settled matters inside it without reference to any court. The Meccan audience knew the arrangement well, since disputes within a clan were normally handled by its chief. No occasion is reported for these ayat. What early scholars stress is the gap the surah leaves open: a true finding is made and no consequence follows from it.

keyTerms.note: The pronoun is feminine plural though only one woman is present. The grammarians note the shift and read it as a general remark rather than an accusation of a group, which is how the classical commentaries take it.
Literally to turn your side towards something. It is the vocabulary of disengagement, not of forgiveness, and it asks Joseph to drop a matter he has just been proved right about.
From a root for missing a mark, used of deliberate fault rather than accident. The brothers use the same word of themselves at the end of the surah, when they finally admit what they did.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Reputation was the currency of that society, and a clan handled it together. A clan took in a member's disgrace or pushed it out. Quiet settlements were preferred to public findings, because a public finding bound everyone. Listeners in Mecca would have known the instinct at once. Keep it inside the walls. Tell the injured party to move on. Let the household's standing come through whole.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for those in the wrong that closes this passage comes back near the end of the surah. There Joseph's brothers use it of themselves and ask their father to seek forgiveness for them. The same term frames both halves of the story. It is spoken once about a woman who is never named, and once by men who are never named.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage separates knowing the truth from acting on it. It shows that the first, without the second, changes very little. A verdict was reached in this room and it protected nobody. That is a sober point about what human bodies of power do. The surah answers it by shape rather than by argument. What is buried here is dug up later, in public, by the person who buried it.

crossReferences.why: The signs were seen, and Joseph is imprisoned anyway, which is where this silence leads.
The same woman states publicly what was settled privately here, and clears him by name.
The brothers use this same word of themselves when they finally ask to be forgiven.

studies.applyIt: Think of something you know to be true about a situation and have not said, because saying it would cost more than staying quiet. You do not have to announce it today. Write down what the cost actually is, in plain words. Most of the time the cost turns out to be smaller and more specific than the fog around it.
studies.explainEasier: The man of the house sees that the shirt is torn at the back, so he knows Joseph is not to blame. He tells Joseph to say no more about it. He tells his wife to ask God to forgive her.

studies.title: Love Has Reached Her Heart
studies.meaning: The story leaves the house and enters the town, and the verb the women use is unusually precise. It says love has got past the outer covering of her heart, an anatomical image rather than a poetic one. Their verdict follows: we see her in plain error. Early scholars note that the talk is not sympathy. It is the ordinary pleasure of judging a household above one's own, and she reads it as the attack it is.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah was heard in a town where reputation moved fast and gossip was a tool of power. The Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) and the early Muslims were themselves the subject of organised talk in Mecca's assemblies. No occasion is reported for this ayah. Early scholars observe that the women name her only by her husband's office. A public figure's household became public property then as now.

keyTerms.note: An indefinite plural for a small group, not the women of the city as a whole. The vagueness is the point: the talk has no author anyone can name, which is what makes it hard to answer.
The noun behind this verb names the membrane enclosing the heart. The image is of love reaching past a protective layer to the organ itself, and the word occurs nowhere else in the Quran.
The exact phrase the brothers used of their father when they judged his affection for Joseph excessive. Twice in this surah someone is declared plainly lost, and both times the charge concerns love.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Water was carried and grain was ground in company. Those were the hours when a town's news was made. Women of the leading households visited one another as seriously as men holding council. A story that reached those rooms reached everyone. Once such a story started there was no way to correct it. You could only drown it out, and that is exactly what she tries next.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb the women use, of love that has reached the covering of the heart, occurs exactly once in the Quran. Its root names one particular layer of tissue in the body. So the sentence is closer to a doctor's note than to a poetic image. That is part of why the classical dictionaries quote this ayah when they define the word.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage treats an unwanted attachment as something that happens inside a person rather than as a choice. It does that without excusing anything. The difference runs through the surah. Strong desire is real, and a person still answers for it. Putting the finding in the mouths of gossips makes a further point. The people most sure about another person's heart are the ones with least access to it.

crossReferences.why: The brothers judged their father in exactly these words, calling his love plain error.
Her answer to this talk: a banquet designed to make the town feel what she felt.
Describes rumour passed from tongue to tongue and treated as trivial while it does real damage.

studies.applyIt: Notice, today, a piece of news about someone you will never meet or never speak to about it. Ask yourself what you gain from holding it. Then let it end with you, once, on purpose. This surah shows a town's talk driving a woman to an act she would not otherwise have attempted.
studies.explainEasier: Word gets out around the town. Some of the women say the governor's wife is chasing her own servant, and that love for him has gone deep into her heart. They say she has clearly lost her way.

studies.title: This Is No Human Being
studies.meaning: She answers gossip with a showing, and the design is exact. Seat the guests on cushions. Put a knife in every hand. Hold their attention with food. Then have him walk in. Their hands are cut and they do not notice. What they say is not a compliment but a mistake about categories. They reach for the only explanation their world offers for something past the human scale. The surah reports it without backing it, and lets the scene make her case for her.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Hospitality on this pattern was familiar to the first hearers, who knew what it meant to seat guests, honour them and place them under obligation. No occasion is reported for this ayah. Early scholars note that she does not deny the women's charge but relocates it: having felt what she felt, they are in no position to judge, and the room's own hands become the evidence.

keyTerms.note: A gathering with cushions where guests lean while eating, and by extension the meal itself. The word appears nowhere else in the Quran, and it signals leisure and comfort as the setting for what follows.
A verb from the root for greatness, meaning to reckon something immense. It describes their judgement rather than their feeling, which is why the sentence that follows is a conclusion drawn aloud.

The phrase occurs only here in the Quran. In their mouths it is a way of saying that no human being looks like this, and the Book elsewhere corrects the assumption that angels would appear in such a form.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Meat was cut at the meal, not before it. Guests were given knives and took portions from a common dish, and a host's standing was measured by what was set down and how many were seated. Cutting yourself at another family's table was a humiliation that would be repeated around the town. She has arranged an occasion where the whole room injures itself in public and cannot complain about it.
studies.didYouKnow: Three of the words in this single ayah occur nowhere else in the Quran. They are the word for a cushioned banquet, the word for a knife, and the phrase a noble angel. It is unusual for one ayah to carry three terms found only there. The crowding matches the scene, which has no parallel anywhere else in the Book.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The women reach for an angel because beauty at this pitch seems to need another kind of being. The Quran records the mistake exactly. Angels in this Book are not glorified humans, and messengers are not more than human. Both points are made again and again elsewhere. The scene also shows how easily a crowd turns amazement into a claim about God. A claim like that then excuses whatever the crowd wants to do next.

crossReferences.why: Answers the demand for an angel by noting that an angel sent to people would have to appear as a man.
These same women testify years later that they knew no evil of him.
States that a messenger sent to people on earth would be a human being, not an angel.

studies.applyIt: Watch, this week, for the moment a room agrees about something all at once. It feels like recognition and it is usually contagion. When you feel it, wait ten seconds before speaking, and say what you actually saw rather than what the room has settled on. The pause is small and it is the whole exercise.
studies.explainEasier: She hears what the women are saying. So she invites them to a meal and gives each one a knife. Then she calls Joseph in. They stare at him, cut their hands, and say he must be an angel.

studies.title: He Held Himself Firm
studies.meaning: She admits everything and threatens him in the same breath. For her, the two halves of the sentence do not clash. The admission is her defence. Look at him, she says, then tell me I was astray. The verb she uses for his refusal is unusually strong. It pictures a man taking hold of something so he cannot be moved. Then comes the threat, spoken in front of witnesses. That turns a private matter into a public one and makes prison a question of her standing.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The first hearers took a threat spoken before witnesses as binding. Words said in company held the speaker to them in a way private words did not. No occasion is reported for this ayah. Early scholars note that the women she invited have now become her backers. That is why the imprisonment follows soon after, even though the household already knew where the fault lay.

keyTerms.note: A form that means to seek protection by gripping something. The root gives the words for a stronghold and for a bond, so the picture is of holding on rather than of merely declining. It occurs once in the Quran.
The verb carries two emphatic markers at once, an opening particle and a closing suffix, which is Arabic at its most insistent. She is not predicting the outcome; she is undertaking to produce it.
Those made small in the eyes of others, from a root about smallness in rank rather than in size. The only other place the Quran uses this form is of a proud creature ordered out of a high station.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Power in that world was mostly the power to arrange outcomes without arguing for them. A chief did not need a court. He needed the agreement of the people who mattered, and that agreement was put together in rooms like this one. Every listener knew a case where an outsider had lost everything because a household decided he should. They knew that being right had not helped him.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb for Joseph's refusal appears only once in the whole Quran, here. The person who says it is the person he refused. His innocence in this scene is settled by her word, not his own, and she gives it twice. Once in this room. Once in public and under oath, many years later, before the king.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Truth survives in the mouths of people with every reason to bury it. She grants the fact and simply refuses what follows from it. That is a recognisable human position rather than a monstrous one. The passage also sets up what the surah says about the cost of staying honest. God honours Joseph's refusal and the world punishes it. The story insists on reporting both.

crossReferences.why: Joseph's immediate answer to the threat, which accepts the prison and asks for help.
The same admission repeated in public years later, this time with nothing left to lose.
States the principle at work: people are not left to say they believe without being tested.

studies.applyIt: Think of a time you were honest about a fact and still refused what followed from it. Everyone has one. Name it to yourself today without any softening, then ask what you would have needed in order to go the rest of the way. The answer is usually smaller than a change of character.
studies.explainEasier: She tells the women that this is the man they blamed her for. She says she did try to make him come to her, and that he said no. Then she warns that he will go to prison if he keeps refusing.

studies.title: Prison Is Dearer To Me
studies.meaning: The prayer is not what a reader expects. Joseph does not ask to be spared, and he does not claim he is strong enough. He states a preference, then asks God to turn the scheming away, then says plainly what he will become if that help is withheld. Early scholars dwell on the honesty of the middle clause. A man who has just refused is telling God that refusal is not something he can guarantee twice.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and heard by people under sustained pressure to give up a commitment in exchange for safety. Some of them had already been offered exactly that trade. No occasion is reported for this ayah. Early scholars read it as the surah's answer to the question such a community would be asking: what does a person pray when both available paths are bad and one of them is prison.

keyTerms.note: The word and its verb occur nine times in this surah and nowhere else in the Quran. Prisons belong to a settled state with walls and officials, which is why the term is confined to the one story set in Egypt.
A verb for leaning, used of a young person's inclination and of a branch bending. It admits a pull without conceding a decision, which is exactly the state Joseph is describing.

In Quranic usage this names a way of acting rather than a lack of information: impulsive, heedless of consequence. Joseph's fear is not that he would be uninformed but that he would behave like someone who is.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Arabia had no prisons. Wrongdoing was answered by payment, by exile, or by blood money. A man who lost a dispute lost property or protection rather than his freedom. Egypt did have prisons. The surah's audience would have heard the detail as foreign and unsettling. It marked a state strong enough to keep a man alive and unfree at the same time.
studies.didYouKnow: Every use of the word for prison in the Quran falls inside this surah. It comes nine times in all, from the first threat to Joseph's own thanks at the end. The term appears in no other surah. That makes surah 12 the only place in the Book with a scene set inside a cell.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The prayer keeps what he wants apart from what he can manage. Joseph knows which option he prefers. He does not assume he can hold to it. The Quran presents that pairing as maturity rather than weakness. It also shows a servant treating God as the one who moves circumstances, not as a supply of willpower. What he asks for is not strength. It is for the pressure itself to be turned away.

crossReferences.why: The immediate answer: the scheming is turned aside, and the response is credited to God.
The same posture in a communal prayer: do not place on us what we have no strength for.
Names the pull this prayer is about, and says mercy is what keeps a soul from following it.

studies.applyIt: Add one line to a prayer this week that admits what you cannot promise. Not a confession and not a resolution, just the plain sentence: without help here, I know what I would do. Most of us pray for outcomes and hide our estimate of ourselves. This ayah shows a prophet handing his over.
studies.explainEasier: Joseph prays to God. He says he would rather go to prison than do what they are asking him to do. He asks God to keep their plan away from him, or he might give in and act foolishly.

studies.title: Answered, And Then Imprisoned
studies.meaning: The prayer is granted in one clause and the prison arrives in the next. God turned the scheming away from him, and then, after they had seen the signs, it occurred to them to shut him up for a time. Nothing has gone wrong. The request was for the pull to be removed, not for the consequences to be, and the surah keeps the two apart. Early scholars note that those deciding know he is innocent; the imprisonment is about their reputation, not his guilt.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The community hearing this had watched the powerful in Mecca concede in private that the message was not what they publicly claimed, and act against it anyway. No occasion is reported for these ayat. Early scholars take the reference to signs as covering the torn shirt, the witness's reasoning and the cut hands together, so the decision is made by people who have already run out of doubts.

keyTerms.note: A form meaning to answer a call that was actually addressed to you. The Quran uses it for God receiving prayer, and the immediacy here comes from the connecting particle, which links answer to request without a gap.

The same word the Book uses for its own verses. Here it means the pieces of proof already produced in the household, and the ayah's force depends on the decision being taken after them rather than before.
Deliberately vague. The noun means a stretch of time of no fixed length, so the sentence hands down a term with no end date, which is the specific cruelty of the decision.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Egypt's officials kept records. They held men without trial and let them go when it suited. Arabian listeners settled their disputes through kin within days. A power that could simply set a matter aside, with no end in view, was foreign to them. There was no elder to appeal to and no clan to pay damages. Time itself became the tool, and nobody had to say for how long.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase closing this passage, for a while, gives no length at all. The surah supplies a figure only later, in a word the classical dictionaries define as a number between three and nine, and even then the Quran never states the exact count of years. The vagueness of the sentence is preserved in the telling of it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: A prayer can be answered exactly and still leave a person in trouble. What was asked for and what was feared are not the same thing. The passage makes that unusually clear. Answer and imprisonment sit in sentences next to each other. It also places the injustice exactly. These men act against evidence they have already accepted, and the Quran treats that throughout as a worse failure than not knowing.
