A comparative that takes the word his sons twice claimed for themselves and gives it to God. The transfer is the whole argument: guardianship is not withdrawn from the world, only relocated.

keyTerms.gloss: the Most Merciful of the merciful
keyTerms.note: A superlative measured against other mercy rather than in isolation. It concedes that people can be merciful and then places God's mercy above the whole class, which is why it is said at the point of letting go.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Sending a son on a journey meant handing him to the desert, to bandits, and to whoever his companions turned out to be. There was no way to check on him and no message until the party returned. Every parent in that audience had done it. The phrase about a better guardian names the only thing available to a person watching a caravan get smaller on the horizon.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase Jacob uses for God as the Most Merciful of the merciful occurs four times in the Quran. Two of those are in this surah. It comes here, when he releases his youngest son, and later in the mouth of Joseph, when he forgives his brothers. Father and son reach for the same words at their two hardest moments.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Trust in God is shown as something a person does with open eyes, not as a substitute for judgement. Jacob knows exactly what these men can do, says so, and still lets the boy go. The alternative is to guard something he cannot guard. The passage also refuses to make reliance a guarantee of outcome. What he names at the end is God's mercy, not a promise about the journey.

crossReferences.why: Joseph closes the reckoning with the same name for God his father used when letting go.
The promise his sons made the first time, using the very word he now takes from them.
What he asks for before agreeing, which is a pledge made before God rather than to him.

studies.applyIt: Think of something you are holding tightly because you do not trust the people who would otherwise carry it. Name honestly why you do not trust them, without softening it. Then hand over one small piece of it anyway, and say a line to God about the part you cannot watch. Both halves belong to this ayah.
studies.explainEasier: Jacob asks his sons how he can trust them with this boy. He trusted them with his brother once, and look what happened. He says God is the best keeper, and the most kind of all who show kindness.

studies.title: What More Could We Want
studies.meaning: The bags are opened and the argument wins itself. Their money is inside, and the sentence that follows is pure salesmanship: what more do we want. Then four benefits in a row. Supplies for the family, a guard on the brother, an extra camel-load, and the whole thing brushed off as easy trade. Early scholars note the ordering. The care of the boy is listed third, between the household's supplies and the extra ration, and nobody in the room seems to notice.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, spoken to a city where a camel-load was a real unit of account. Everyone there knew what one extra load meant to a family in a lean season. No occasion is reported for this ayah. Early scholars note that the returned payment does just what Joseph intended. It turns the second journey from a risk their father must accept into an offer the household cannot refuse.

keyTerms.note: A question that closes discussion rather than opening it. The verb means to seek or to want, and framing the request this way makes any remaining objection sound like ingratitude.

keyTerms.gloss: and we will provision our family
keyTerms.note: A specific verb for fetching food supplies for dependants. It names the errand's real purpose in one word, and it is the first of the four benefits they list.

The adjective means small, light or readily obtained, and early scholars read it both ways: a modest amount not worth refusing, or a quantity easy to come by. Either reading makes the request sound trivial.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Rationing during a shortage was done per head. One more man in the party meant one more camel-load of grain. For a large household that was the difference between eating through a season and running out before it ended. The arithmetic was public and everybody could do it. That is why the brothers can make their case in a single sentence and expect it to land.
studies.didYouKnow: Their list of reasons puts the youngest brother's safety third of four. It comes after supplies for the household and before an extra camel-load of grain. The surah reports the order without comment and never returns to it. The ordering is left to do its own work on a listener who has been following this family since its first council.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage shows how an unexpected gift becomes an argument. Nothing they say is false. The whole speech is shaped by the relief of finding money they thought they had spent. The Quran is often exact about this. Sudden ease loosens judgement, and a good turn received can be the very thing that carries people into a decision they had been resisting for sound reasons.

crossReferences.why: The instruction that put the money there, and the effect it was designed to have.
Their father's answer, which refuses the arithmetic and asks for something binding instead.
Names wealth and children as a trial, which is precisely the pressure operating in this room.

studies.applyIt: Watch for the sentence what more could we want in your own mouth this week. It usually arrives just after something unexpectedly good and just before a decision. When you hear it, name the thing that is actually being risked, out loud, once. Then decide. Often the decision is the same and it is now yours.
studies.explainEasier: They open their bags and find that their money has been put back. They tell their father there is nothing more to ask for. With their brother along, they can bring food home and get one more camel-load.

studies.title: A Pledge Before God
studies.meaning: He stops accepting promises and asks for something else. He wants a binding undertaking taken in God's name, with one exception written into it. Unless you are overwhelmed. That clause is the interesting part. It grants in advance that circumstances can defeat honest men, so the pledge is not a guarantee nobody could keep. When they give it, he does not thank them. He says God is witness over what we say, which puts the agreement where neither party can quietly revise it.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Oaths sworn in God's name were the strongest tool that society had, stronger than any writing. Breaking one destroyed a man's standing for good. No occasion is reported for this ayah. Early scholars read Jacob's insistence as the natural response of a man whose sons' loose assurances had already failed once. They note that he asks for the pledge only after stating his condition plainly.

keyTerms.note: From the root for tying firmly, the same root behind the words for a rope and for a covenant. It names an obligation with a knot in it, not an intention, which is what he had been given before.
A passive verb meaning to be encircled with no way out. The exception covers being overpowered by events rather than changing your mind, and it is written into the pledge by the person demanding it.
The one to whom a matter is committed for keeping. Naming God as witness over the words themselves places the pledge beyond the reach of both parties, including the father who asked for it.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Contracts in that world were spoken and witnessed. Two men clasped hands in front of others and called on God. The deal held because everyone present would remember it and repeat it. Writing existed but was rare and mostly for trade. The one thing stronger than a written record was a public oath. The one thing that ended a man socially was being known to have broken one.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for the binding pledge in this ayah occurs three times in the Quran, and all three are in this surah. Twice here, as Jacob takes it. Once later, when the eldest brother recalls it in Egypt and refuses to leave. A single term carries the obligation from the moment it is given to the moment it is honoured.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Trust between people is shown needing a third party, and the surah puts God in that place rather than any human authority. The exception clause matters just as much. An undertaking that admitted no limits would either be broken or would force the brothers into an impossible spot. Building the limit into the oath is what makes it honest. Being realistic about what people can do is treated here as part of good faith.

crossReferences.why: The eldest brother remembers this pledge in Egypt and refuses to leave because of it.
The informal promise this replaces, which repeated a form of words already broken once.
Addresses covenants made in God's name and the weight carried by making Him the guarantor.

studies.applyIt: When you next agree to something that matters, build the exception in out loud. Say what would actually stop you, in one clause, at the moment of agreeing. It feels like weakening the promise and it does the opposite. Everyone knows the exception exists; naming it is what makes the rest of the sentence believable.
studies.explainEasier: Jacob says he will not send the boy until they give him a promise before God. They must swear to bring him back, unless something stops them that they cannot fight. They swear, and he calls God a witness.

studies.title: Enter By Different Gates
studies.meaning: A practical instruction is given and then at once stripped of any power. Do not go in as one group. Enter separately. Then, in the same breath: I cannot protect you from God in anything. Early scholars generally read the advice as a precaution against being noticed. They note that Jacob takes the trouble to say his own precaution guarantees nothing. The ayah ends by moving from what he does to what he relies on, and then widens from himself to everyone who relies.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Eleven brothers arriving together at a foreign city's gate would have stood out. Travelling parties often split up to avoid notice, tolls or trouble. No occasion is reported for this ayah. Some early scholars mention the evil eye and others simple caution about drawing attention. The surah names neither, and the classical discussions record the range without settling it.

keyTerms.note: The adjective is the one Joseph used in prison of scattered lords. Here dispersal is prudent and there it was the objection, so the same word carries opposite value in two mouths.
A verb for warding off need or harm. Jacob uses it of himself, which is unusual advice to attach to your own instructions, and it is the reason the ayah is not simply about tactics.
From the root for appointing an agent to act on your behalf. Reliance in this vocabulary is a delegation rather than a mood, which is why it sits so comfortably next to giving practical instructions.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: City gates were where rulers met travellers. Tolls were taken and strangers were questioned. A large party from outside the country drew just the interest nobody wanted. Caravans often broke up before they arrived and gathered again inside. To the first hearers this would have sounded like plain road sense. It came from a man who had been sending sons on journeys all his life.
studies.didYouKnow: The sentence about judgement belonging to God alone, which Jacob uses here, also appears earlier in this surah. There it is spoken by Joseph in an Egyptian prison. Neither of them knows the other is alive. The Quran gives father and son the same words, in the same surah, in settings as different as a cell and a departure at home.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Reliance on God is defined here by what it does not replace. Jacob gives sensible instructions and then denies that his instructions can protect anyone. Both halves are presented as belonging together. The passage rules out two errors at once. One is thinking that taking care shows a lack of faith. The other is thinking that taking care is what keeps you safe. The last clause turns the whole thing into a rule for anyone who relies.

crossReferences.why: Joseph uses the identical sentence about judgement, years earlier and in a prison.
The narration's verdict on this advice: it availed them nothing, but it settled something in him.
Messengers under threat give the same closing formula about where the reliant should rely.

studies.applyIt: Do the sensible thing this week and say the other half out loud. Lock the door, then say plainly that the lock is not what keeps the house. Send the application, then say the same about the application. Most people do one or the other. Doing both in one motion is the shape this ayah is describing.
studies.explainEasier: Jacob tells his sons not to go into the city by one gate. He says they should enter by different gates. He adds that he cannot keep them safe from God. God decides, and Jacob puts his trust in him.

studies.title: A Need In Jacob's Soul
studies.meaning: The verdict on the previous instruction is blunt: it availed them nothing against God. Then the ayah says what it did do, and the phrase is unusually tender. It was a need in Jacob's soul, which he settled. Early scholars read this as neither praise nor blame but plain description. A father did what he could, the doing changed no outcome, and it answered something in him. The closing clause says he had knowledge because God taught him, and that most people do not know.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah's first hearers were people making small arrangements against very large pressures, and this ayah speaks to that directly. No occasion is reported for it. Early scholars note the unusual move of the narration judging a prophet's advice while backing his knowledge in the same breath. They read it as separating the limits of a precaution from the standing of the person taking it.

keyTerms.note: The word covers a want, an errand and an unmet requirement at once. Applied to an inner state it names something a person has to discharge before they can rest, whether or not it changes anything outside.
The verb for completing something owed, used of debts and of decrees. It says the need was not merely felt but paid off, which is why the sentence reads as sympathetic rather than dismissive.

The same verb used at the surah's opening for what God would teach Joseph. Knowledge in this story is consistently traced back to a teacher, in both generations, and never treated as native shrewdness.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Everyone in that world knew the small rituals people perform when someone leaves. The words said at a departure. The way a bag is packed. The last instruction called after a rider. None of them keep anyone safe on a desert road, and everyone does them anyway. The ayah names that human behaviour exactly and does not mock it, which is why the sentence has stayed memorable.
studies.didYouKnow: This is one of the few places in the Quran where the narration comments directly on whether a prophet's own advice worked. It says plainly that the advice changed nothing. In the same ayah it says he had knowledge from God. The two statements are set side by side with no attempt to square them.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Knowing a great deal sits fine with acting on a limited plan, and the passage refuses to make that a contradiction. Jacob's knowledge is real and God-given. It does not stretch to controlling what happens at a foreign city gate. The ayah also grants dignity to the human need that produces such precautions. Doing what you can is treated as something a person owes themselves, quite apart from whether it works.

crossReferences.why: The instruction this ayah judges, along with Jacob's own disclaimer about its power.
Jacob says again that he knows from God what his sons do not know.
Returns to the same theme: above every possessor of knowledge is one who knows more.

studies.applyIt: Think of a small thing you do that cannot possibly affect the outcome, and that you would feel wrong skipping. Checking the door twice, a phrase you say when someone drives off. You do not need to defend it or stop it. This ayah says a need was settled, and leaves that as a real thing that happened.
studies.explainEasier: The sons went in the way their father told them. It did not keep them safe from what God had decided. It only settled something Jacob felt inside. God had taught him, though most people do not know.

studies.title: I Am Your Brother
studies.meaning: The disclosure is made to one person and kept from ten. He draws his brother to himself, says who he is, and adds a single instruction: do not grieve over what they used to do. Early scholars note what is absent. There is no explanation, no plan shared, no request for secrecy stated in the text, and no promise about how this ends. What the younger brother is given is a fact and a permission to stop carrying something, which is all the scene contains.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The first audience read it alongside their own experience of families split by the new message, where some members knew things others could not be told. No occasion is reported for this ayah. Early scholars observe that the youngest brother has grown up in the household that lost Joseph. That is the situation the instruction about grief is addressed to.

keyTerms.note: A verb for taking someone into shelter, used of giving refuge as well as of an embrace. It occurs twice in this surah and both are reunions: this one, and later when his parents arrive in Egypt.
Three words with no title, no office and no account of the intervening years. The most powerful man in Egypt identifies himself by the one relation that has no rank attached to it.
A form of the verb for hardship and misery, meaning to be brought low by grief. The negation is gentle rather than commanding, closer to you need not than to you should not.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A younger brother in a large household grew up inside a story he had not seen. He would have heard about the missing son at every gathering. He would have watched his father's grief become a fixed feature of the house. He knew he was the surviving half of a pair. Everyone in that audience understood how a family's central loss shapes the childhood of whoever comes afterwards.
studies.didYouKnow: The verb used here for drawing someone into shelter occurs twice in this surah and nowhere else in it. Both occurrences are reunions in the same room in Egypt: first when Joseph takes his brother to himself, and later, thirty ayat on, when he does the same for his parents. The word bookends the family's return.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage separates relief from resolution. Nothing about the brothers' guilt is settled here and nothing is forgiven. One person is simply released from grieving over it. That difference runs through the surah, which keeps giving people what they need before it gives them what they are owed. It also shows a man with total power over his family choosing, for the moment, to use it on one person's sorrow.

crossReferences.why: The same verb of shelter used again, when his parents finally reach him in Egypt.
Where the disclosure is finally made to everyone, and the reckoning is opened and closed.
Their father, still in Canaan, sending them out with the same refusal to give up on grief.

studies.applyIt: There is someone carrying a family sadness that is not really theirs: a younger sibling, a child, someone who arrived after the difficult years. Tell them one true thing this week that they were not told at the time. Not the whole account. One fact, and permission to stop holding the part that was never theirs.
studies.explainEasier: The brothers come in to Joseph. He takes his own brother close to him and tells him who he is. He says he is his brother, and that he should not be sad about what the others used to do.

studies.title: The Announcer Called Out
studies.meaning: Two actions and a shout. The cup goes into the saddlebag, the caravan leaves, and then a voice behind them calls the whole party thieves. The surah is careful about who speaks: an announcer announced, with Joseph's name attached to neither the cry nor the accusation. Commentators note that no false statement is put in Joseph's mouth anywhere in this episode, and that the arrangement is described as devised for him rather than by him a few ayat later.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Public proclamation was how anything official reached a crowd, and a called accusation carried real force because everyone within earshot became a witness to it. No occasion is reported for this ayah. The commentators discuss at length how a prophet could be part of such a stratagem, and the surah's own answer arrives later, where the plan is attributed to God rather than to Joseph's cleverness.

keyTerms.note: A word for a vessel used for giving drink, and also for a place where water is provided. It occurs only here in the Quran, and the same object is named with a different word two ayat later.
A verb followed by the doer of the same verb, from the root for hearing and for giving public notice. The construction keeps the speaker anonymous while making the act itself formal and official.
The word is for the animals and their loads rather than the people, so the cry is addressed to the convoy as a body. Their father uses the same word much later when he senses Joseph on the air.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A caravan leaving a city was pursued easily and stopped without difficulty, since loaded animals move slowly and the road was known. Everyone travelling knew the risk of an accusation at departure, when goods had been handled by strangers and nobody could prove what had been packed by whom. Reputation was the only defence, and these men had no reputation in Egypt at all.
studies.didYouKnow: The vessel at the centre of this episode is named twice with two different words, and each of them occurs only once in the whole Quran. One is a word for a drinking vessel, the other for a measuring bowl. The object that decides the story's turning point is described so precisely that neither term is ever needed again.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage is careful about attribution in a way the reader may not notice at first. Joseph places an object; an unnamed man makes a claim; the claim is not repeated by Joseph and is never confirmed by the narration. That precision matters because the surah is about to say who really devised this, and the answer removes the question of a prophet's deceit by relocating the plan entirely.

crossReferences.why: Names the author of the stratagem, and says Joseph could not have done this by the king's law.
The earlier use of the same saddlebags, when what was hidden in them was a kindness.
Their father uses the same word for the caravan when he senses that something has changed.

studies.applyIt: Notice how often the harshest version of a thing gets said by someone other than the person who arranged it: a message passed on, a rule quoted, a decision announced by a junior. When you are the one arranging, say it yourself. When you are the one announcing, ask whose sentence you are carrying.

studies.title: By God, We Are Not Thieves
studies.meaning: Three short ayat of exchange, and the brothers' answer is the one worth pausing on. They turn towards the accusers, ask what is missing, hear the reward offered for its return, and then swear. Their defence is not evidence but character: you know we did not come here to cause trouble. Commentators note the irony of the oath, since these are men who once sold a brother and brought a shirt home soaked in false blood, and who are now, on this particular charge, entirely innocent.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. An oath sworn in God's name was the strongest defence available to a man with no witnesses, and the surah's first audience would have weighed it that way. No occasion is reported for these ayat. The commentators point out that the brothers appeal to how they have conducted themselves in Egypt over two visits, which is the only evidence a foreign trader could offer for anything.

keyTerms.note: An oath particle used for surprise or strong denial, less common than the ordinary one. It occurs nine times in the Quran, and four of those fall in this surah, always at a moment of protest.
The standard large unit of measure for grain in that world. Offering one as a reward makes the search official and public, and puts a price on the object that everyone present can understand.
Someone who personally stands surety for a debt or a claim. The word occurs twice in the Quran, and using it here turns a reward into a formal undertaking rather than an offer.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Theft from a host was among the worst things a traveller could be accused of, because the whole system of caravan trade rested on strangers being able to eat and sleep in each other's territory. A party found guilty would not trade in that market again, and the news would follow them home. The brothers are not only defending themselves; they are defending their ability to come back for grain.
studies.didYouKnow: The particular oath the brothers swear here, an emphatic by God used in protest and astonishment, appears nine times in the Quran and four of those are in this surah. They use it now to deny a theft, and they will use it twice more before the story ends, once to reproach their father and once to admit that they were wrong all along.
studies.theologicalSignificance: A true statement made by unreliable people is still true, and the surah insists on it. These men are innocent of this charge and their oath is honest, which the narrative allows without softening anything about their history. It also shows the limits of character as evidence. Their defence is that people who behave as they have behaved do not steal, and it happens to be correct and would not have saved them.

crossReferences.why: The same men once claimed truthfulness while lying; here they claim it while telling the truth.
Their confidence leads them straight into naming a penalty they will have to accept.
The same oath used a third time, when they finally admit what they had denied for years.

studies.applyIt: Think of someone whose word you discount because of something they once did. Test yourself this week: when they tell you something checkable, check it rather than assuming. People are unreliable in patterns, not uniformly, and treating a person as wrong by default is its own kind of inaccuracy.

studies.title: They Named Their Own Penalty
studies.meaning: The Egyptians ask what the punishment should be if the denial proves false, and the brothers supply it themselves. Whoever's bag holds it becomes the property of the wronged party. Commentators explain that this was the practice of their own homeland rather than Egyptian law, which is precisely why the question was asked in that form. Confidence in their innocence produces the exact outcome Joseph needs, and the trap closes with the brothers' own sentence rather than with a judge's.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Different peoples had different customs for theft, and travellers were commonly judged by their own law when they could state it, which is why the question is put to them rather than answered by an official. No occasion is reported for these ayat. The commentators treat the exchange as a legal procedure rather than a trick, since the brothers are asked and answer freely.

keyTerms.note: A word for the return owed for an act, good or bad. It appears three times in two short ayat, so the question and the answer are built from a single repeated term, which gives the exchange its ring of formality.
The same pack that carried the returned payment on the first journey. Twice in this surah a family's fate is decided by what is discovered inside travelling gear at the end of a road.
From a root meaning to put a thing where it does not belong. The brothers use the general word rather than a word for thieves, which widens their sentence beyond the charge in front of them.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Custom varied sharply between peoples, and a traveller's best protection was being able to say what his own law prescribed. Among some communities a thief became bonded to the person he stole from until the debt was cleared. Egyptian practice was different. Asking the accused to state their own rule was therefore a recognised procedure, not an ambush, and every listener would have known it as such.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for recompense appears three times across these two short ayat, twice inside a single sentence where the brothers say that his recompense is that he himself is the recompense. Arabic can turn a phrase back on itself like this, and the repetition makes their answer sound like a formula recited rather than a judgement improvised.
studies.theologicalSignificance: People are shown sentencing themselves out of certainty, and the surah presents this as a general hazard rather than a peculiar misfortune. The brothers are confident because they are innocent, and their confidence is what binds them. The passage also raises a question the next ayah answers directly: whether what is happening here is Joseph's cleverness or something else operating through an ordinary legal exchange.

crossReferences.why: Names who devised this, and says Joseph could not have taken his brother under Egyptian law.
The oath whose confidence leads directly into the sentence they pronounce here.
Joseph holds them to their own rule and refuses to substitute anyone else for the accused.

studies.applyIt: Notice this week when you are about to answer a question with more certainty than you have checked. What would I do if that ever happened is the same shape as the sentence these men produce. Before you answer, add one clause: assuming I have this right. It costs nothing and it leaves you a door.

studies.title: Above Every Knower, One Knowing
studies.meaning: The search is staged so that nothing looks arranged: the other bags first, the youngest brother's last. Then the narration steps forward and takes the plan away from Joseph. Thus We devised for Joseph. He could not have detained his brother under the king's law unless God willed it, so the whole manoeuvre is credited elsewhere. The closing sentence widens beyond the scene entirely, and it is one of the most quoted lines in the surah: above every possessor of knowledge is one who knows more.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, addressed to people whose opponents were confident they had understood the situation and were arranging matters accordingly. No occasion is reported for this ayah. The commentators use it to answer the question raised by the previous scene, since the word for devising is the surah's recurring term for covert contrivance, and here the Quran attaches it to God rather than to a prophet's own ingenuity.

keyTerms.note: The surah's word for working indirectly, used until now of brothers plotting and of a household scheming. Applied to God it means the arrangement of events towards an end, without the deceit the human uses carry.

The word usually rendered as religion also means the code by which a people is judged. Here it plainly means Egyptian law, and the phrase records that Joseph was operating inside a legal system not his own.
The noun means steps or ranks, from the root for a staircase. Elevation in this vocabulary happens in increments rather than at once, which describes exactly how the surah has raised Joseph.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Searching a caravan's baggage was a public event conducted in front of the whole party, since a search done privately proved nothing. Order mattered: beginning with the accused looked like foreknowledge, and beginning elsewhere looked fair. Every trader in that audience had stood beside his packs while someone else's hands went through them, and knew how much the sequence of a search was watched.
studies.didYouKnow: The sentence that closes this ayah, that above every possessor of knowledge there is one who knows, occurs only here in the Quran. It arrives in the middle of a domestic scene about a missing cup rather than in a passage about revelation or creation, which is characteristic of how this surah places its largest statements.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah answers the moral question the episode raises by moving the agency. What looked like a prophet's stratagem is described as God's arrangement, worked through a legal exchange the brothers entered freely. It also sets a limit on every human vantage point, including Joseph's. He is being raised by degrees, and the last clause makes clear that no degree reached is the top of the stairs.

crossReferences.why: The same word for devising, used at the surah's opening of what brothers might do to a boy.
Joseph credits the whole sequence to God's subtle kindness once he can see it complete.
Gives the prayer that follows from this sentence: ask for an increase in knowledge.

studies.applyIt: Pick the area where you are genuinely the most knowledgeable person in your circle. Find one person this month who knows more than you about it and ask them a real question, not a polite one. The habit is easy to lose precisely where you are strongest, which is where this ayah is aimed.

studies.title: He Kept It To Himself
studies.meaning: Their first instinct under pressure is to disown the boy and to drag an absent brother in with him. If he has stolen, one of his brothers stole before. The ayah then does something rare: it reports what Joseph did not say. He concealed it within himself and did not disclose it to them, and only afterwards speaks, and even then in a sentence they cannot decode. Commentators note that the reader is given access to an interior the characters in the room do not have.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The remark about an earlier theft has no basis in anything the surah has narrated, and the commentators record several attempts to explain it, none of them agreed upon. What is not disputed is the manoeuvre: a family under suspicion protects itself by separating out the two sons of one mother. No occasion is reported for this ayah.

keyTerms.note: A verb for keeping something inside, from the root behind secrets and behind the inner self. The pronoun has no clear antecedent, so what he concealed is left for the reader to supply.
The opposite verb, meaning to bring into the open. Placing both halves in one sentence makes the silence deliberate and active rather than a simple absence of speech.

keyTerms.gloss: you are in a worse position
keyTerms.note: A comparative about standing rather than about character. It says more than they can hear, since only Joseph and the reader know which position is being compared with which.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Half-brothers in a large polygamous household were a recognised fault line. Full brothers shared a mother's tent, her attention and her interests, and disputes ran along those lines when a family was under strain. Everyone listening had watched a family divide exactly this way, and would have heard the brothers' sentence as the oldest move in that repertoire rather than as anything new.
studies.didYouKnow: The Quran rarely reports the unspoken thoughts of anyone in a narrative, and this ayah does it twice in one clause, saying both that Joseph concealed something and that he did not disclose it. The object of both verbs is a bare pronoun with nothing to attach to, so the tradition offers several suggestions for what exactly he kept in.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Restraint is presented as an act with content, not as an absence. Joseph has evidence, standing and a room full of people who have just handed him an opening, and the ayah spends its central clause on what he did with all of that, which was nothing. The passage also observes how easily a group under threat sacrifices its weakest member, and names that as the worse position of the two.

crossReferences.why: The moment he finally says what he has been holding, and even then he asks rather than accuses.
What the concealment was eventually for, once he had the power to do the opposite.
Names patient restraint after being wronged as among the resolutions worth holding to.

studies.applyIt: The next time someone hands you an opening they do not realise they have handed you, notice the gap before you answer. You do not have to be noble about it. Just let one exchange go by without using what you have. Then decide later, when the heat is out of it, whether it ever needed using.

studies.title: He Has A Very Old Father
studies.meaning: The plea changes tactics completely. Having just distanced themselves from the boy, they now argue for him, and the argument is not about guilt at all. He has a father, a very old man; take one of us instead. Then a compliment that is also a lever: we see you as one who does good. Commentators note that the brothers are for the first time in the surah offering to bear something on someone else's behalf, and that they do it out of fear of their father rather than love of their brother.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Substituting one person for another in a penalty was a recognised idea in that world, since obligations attached to families rather than only to individuals, and a clan could offer a man in place of a man. No occasion is reported for this ayah. The commentators observe that the brothers appeal to Joseph's own reputation, which by now was established well enough for foreigners to have heard of it.

keyTerms.note: A title of high office, from a root for strength and scarcity. The Quran uses it of God elsewhere, and here it addresses the man holding Egypt's stores, which the brothers use as a form of respect.
Two words for age piled up for emphasis. The doubling is not redundant in Arabic; it presses the point, and the point is the only argument they have, since they cannot argue about the cup.

keyTerms.gloss: one of those who do good
keyTerms.note: The surah's measure of a person, used earlier by the two prisoners about Joseph. The brothers now apply it to him without knowing who he is, so the description follows him from a cell to a court.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Old age carried real claims in that society. An elderly parent's needs bound a whole family, and a son who failed one was disgraced publicly. When these men invoke their father's age, they are not appealing to sentiment; they are naming an obligation any listener would recognise as binding. It is also the first time in the surah that they mention his feelings without wanting something from him.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase the brothers use of Joseph here, one who does good, was used of him by his fellow prisoners many years earlier, in almost the same words. Neither group knows the other. The description follows him from a cell to a governorship without anyone in the surah repeating it deliberately, which is how the story records a settled reputation.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage shows a partial change and refuses to inflate it. These are men who abandoned a brother to a well and who moments earlier disowned this one, and who are now willing to take a punishment in his place. The Quran reports the improvement without pronouncing them reformed. Character in this surah moves slowly, under pressure, and by increments the story is content to leave incomplete.

crossReferences.why: The prisoners use the same description of Joseph long before he has any standing at all.
The eldest takes the argument further, refusing to leave the country without the boy.
Sets out the weight of an aged parent's claim, which is the whole force of this plea.

studies.applyIt: Offer to carry one thing this week that is not yours to carry: a task, a difficult phone call, an errand someone is dreading. Do not announce it as a favour. Notice, afterwards, whether it was easier than you expected. Most people find the reluctance was larger than the errand.

studies.title: God Forbid We Should Do That
studies.meaning: The refusal uses the same words he used as a young man in a locked house. God forbid. Then a reason that costs him something: taking anyone other than the person with whom the property was found would make us wrongdoers. He has every reason to accept the substitution, since he wants the youngest brother kept, and he refuses because the offered arrangement would be unjust to whoever volunteered. Commentators note the consistency: the boy stays, and he stays by the rule the brothers themselves stated.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Substituting one man for another was ordinary practice where obligations ran through families, so the brothers' offer was reasonable and would have been accepted by most officials. No occasion is reported for this ayah. The commentators read Joseph's refusal as holding to the rule already agreed in front of witnesses, which is what keeps the whole episode within a legal frame rather than a personal one.

keyTerms.note: The phrase occurs twice in the Quran and both are Joseph's, here and in the governor's house decades earlier. He reaches for the same shelter when refusing what is wrong and when refusing what is easy.
The same word the brothers used long ago for the belongings they claimed to have left Joseph guarding. It runs through the surah for portable things people leave, lose, carry and are accused over.

From putting a thing where it does not belong. Punishing a volunteer in place of the accused would be exactly that displacement, and Joseph names it with the same word the brothers used for their own rule.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Collective responsibility ran deep. A clan paid for its member's crime, a man could stand in for a kinsman's debt, and hostages were given as sureties without anyone thinking it strange. What Joseph declines here would have looked to most listeners like a normal and even generous arrangement, which is why his refusal is striking rather than obvious in that setting.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase Joseph uses to take refuge occurs exactly twice in the Quran, both in this surah and both from him. The first is spoken by a young servant with no power, refusing a woman who could have him imprisoned. The second is spoken by the man who governs Egypt's stores, refusing an offer that would have suited him.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Integrity is shown to be indifferent to circumstance. The same formula appears at the bottom and at the top of his life, in one case protecting him and in the other costing him nothing he wanted. That symmetry is the surah's quiet argument about character: it is what stays the same when the situation reverses completely. The refusal also insists that a desired outcome does not license an unjust means.

crossReferences.why: The first use of the same refuge, spoken as a servant with nothing to fall back on.
The rule the brothers stated themselves, which Joseph now holds to rather than setting aside.
Warns against letting hostility or preference push anyone away from acting fairly.

studies.applyIt: Find the place where the outcome you want could be reached by a shortcut nobody would object to. A small unfairness that suits everyone. Take the long way once this week, without explaining why to anyone. The point is not the outcome, which will probably be the same. It is knowing which of the two roads you took.

studies.title: I Will Not Leave This Land
studies.meaning: They give up and withdraw to confer privately, and the eldest says the thing nobody has said aloud for decades. There are two obligations, he tells them: the pledge you gave before God, and what you did to Joseph. Naming the second is the change. Then he binds himself: I will not leave this country until my father permits me or God decides for me. Commentators note that this is the first time any of them accepts a consequence rather than arranging one.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. A man refusing to return home until a matter was settled was making a public and expensive commitment, since a trading party could not wait and his family would learn of it from the others. No occasion is reported for this ayah. The commentators note that the eldest is not named, as none of the brothers is, and that his speech is reported at unusual length for a figure the surah leaves anonymous.

keyTerms.note: An intensified form of the verb for despairing, meaning to give up entirely after trying. The same verb returns at the surah's very end, describing messengers on the point of despair before help arrives.
The second word describes people in confidential conversation. The first means they separated themselves out, so the phrase pictures a group physically drawing apart from everyone else to speak.

keyTerms.gloss: the best of those who judge
keyTerms.note: A superlative among judges rather than a denial that others judge. He is choosing whose verdict he will wait for, which is what turns his refusal to leave from stubbornness into something else.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A caravan kept its own schedule. Animals had to be fed, the road had seasons, and a man who stayed behind in a foreign country was cut off from everything: no money coming, no way to send word, no protection. Staying was not a gesture. It meant living as a stranger in Egypt indefinitely, and everybody in the surah's first audience understood the arithmetic of that decision.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for the binding pledge their father took occurs three times in the Quran and all three are in this surah. Two are at the moment it is given and the third is here, when the eldest brother recalls it in Egypt. A single term traces the obligation from a tent in Canaan to a decision made in a foreign country.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Repentance is shown beginning as accurate memory. Nothing is confessed and nobody is forgiven; what changes is that an old wrong is finally named in the present tense, alongside a present obligation, by someone who counts them as the same kind of thing. The passage also gives a working definition of trusting God's judgement: a man stops managing the outcome and waits for a decision that is not his to make.

crossReferences.why: The pledge he is recalling, given before God with an exception written into it.
The same verb for despair returns at the surah's close, applied to messengers before help arrives.
Where this naming of the old wrong finally becomes an outright request for forgiveness.

studies.applyIt: Say the old thing out loud to the person who was there. Not an apology yet, and not an explanation. Just the sentence naming what happened, in the plainest words, with no defence attached. Most reconciliations stall long before the apology, at the point where nobody will say the event.

studies.title: We Could Not Guard The Unseen
studies.meaning: The report they are told to carry is unusually careful. It states the finding without vouching for it, adds that they testify only to what they know, and then concedes the limit: we were not keepers of the unseen. Commentators note the contrast with their first homecoming, when they invented a wolf and produced a shirt. This time they offer verification instead, telling their father to ask the town and the caravan. The men who once manufactured evidence now point him towards witnesses.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Checking an account by asking a settlement or a travelling party was the normal method of verification, since news moved with people and a caravan carried the reputation of everyone in it. No occasion is reported for these ayat. The commentators note that the invitation to ask others is exactly what an honest report offers and a fabricated one avoids.

keyTerms.note: They report the charge in the bare form it was made in, without endorsing it or defending against it. The whole care of the message lies in what the following clause does to this one.
The word for guardian that they twice claimed for themselves, now used to name the one thing they were never able to be. It is the surah's most exact correction of their earlier promises.
A town is told to be asked, meaning its people. Arabic often names a place for its inhabitants, and here the figure of speech widens the invitation from a few travellers to everyone who was there.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: News travelled with caravans and settled in towns, where anyone arriving could ask what had happened and expect several versions within an hour. Verification meant finding people with no stake in the story, which is precisely what the brothers are proposing. Their father had no other method available to him, and the offer of it is the substance of their message rather than a flourish.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for guardian returns here for the third time in the surah, always from these same men. Twice they claimed to be guardians of a brother, and both times the claim failed. Here they use it to name a limit instead: nobody can guard what cannot be seen, which is the one true statement they have ever made with that word.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Honesty about the limits of testimony is presented as part of honesty itself. A witness who claims more than he saw is not being more helpful but less reliable, and the surah puts that principle into the mouths of men who once told an unverifiable story. The passage also marks real change without announcing it. The proof of it is not a confession but a change in how they handle information.

crossReferences.why: Their first homecoming report, invented in detail and offering nothing anyone could check.
The guardian claim they made about Joseph, which this ayah quietly withdraws.
Their father's reply, which answers this message the way he answered the first one.

studies.applyIt: Next time you pass on something you were told, mark the seam. This is what I saw; this is what I was told; this part I am guessing. Three short phrases. People who do this are believed more, not less, and it takes about four extra words in an ordinary sentence.

studies.title: Perhaps He Will Bring Them All
studies.meaning: One word gives the old man away. He hopes God will bring them all back to him, and the plural cannot mean two. Commentators have long read that word as evidence that he never believed the story about a wolf and has been waiting for three sons, not one. The ayah opens by repeating, syllable for syllable, the sentence he spoke the first time his sons came home without a brother. Decades apart, in the same words, he refuses the account and does not accuse anyone of anything.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and heard by people who had been waiting years for a change with no sign of one. No occasion is reported for this ayah. The commentators note that Jacob has now lost three sons in effect, two in Egypt and one long ago, and that his response contains no reproach at all, which they read as the reason the surah puts the same words in his mouth twice.

keyTerms.note: A plural covering the whole group. Two sons are missing in Egypt, so the word reaches past them to include one more, and it is the strongest indication in the surah of what he has believed all along.
A particle of expectation rather than certainty, used elsewhere in the Quran for what may be hoped from God. It keeps his hope from becoming a claim, which is what makes it durable.
The name he ends on, paired with the Knowing. Wisdom in this vocabulary is about putting things in their right place, so he closes by naming the arranging rather than the knowing alone.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: An old man in that world was not left alone with his losses. A household lived together, and grief was witnessed daily by everyone under the same roof. There was no separate room to break down in and no way to keep counsel. A father who received bad news twice in a lifetime did so in front of the same audience, and both times had to answer them within the hour.
studies.didYouKnow: The sentence he uses about his sons' own selves contriving something occurs exactly twice in the Quran, and both are his: once when they came home with a bloodied shirt, and once here. The Book offers no reminder of the earlier occasion. A listener who has been following the surah simply hears it come round again.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Hope is shown holding a shape that facts do not support and that the story eventually vindicates. The passage does not present this as denial, because he never disputes what happened; he disputes the account offered for it. That distinction is what keeps the ayah from being about optimism. What he expects is not a good outcome in general but a specific arrangement by a God he names as knowing and wise.

crossReferences.why: The identical sentence, spoken the first time his sons came home a brother short.
The instruction that follows from this hope: go and search, and do not despair.
The all of them arriving, when the whole household enters Egypt together.

studies.applyIt: Notice a hope you are carrying that you have stopped saying out loud because it embarrasses you. Say it once this week to one person, in a plain sentence, without arguing for it. You do not have to defend the odds. Jacob states his in eight words and then names God twice.

studies.title: His Eyes Turned White
studies.meaning: He turns away from them and cries out a name, and the name is not the son just lost in Egypt. It is Joseph. Decades of composure end in one syllable of grief. Then two clauses that sit oddly together: his eyes whitened from sorrow, and he was one who holds it in. The Arabic word means a person swallowing what he feels rather than one who has stopped feeling it. Commentators generally read the whitening as blindness brought on by weeping.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and heard during years the tradition remembers as heavy with loss for the community and for the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) personally. No occasion is reported for this ayah. The commentators note that the surah has withheld any description of Jacob's inner state until now, reporting only his speech, and that this is the single place where his body is described rather than his words.

keyTerms.note: A cry addressing grief itself as though it were present in the room. The word covers sorrow mixed with anger at a loss, and this exclamation occurs nowhere else in the Quran.
A verb for becoming white, used of eyes only here. The commentators read it as sight failing after prolonged weeping, and the ayah gives the cause plainly as sorrow rather than age.
From a root for tying up the mouth of a waterskin so nothing escapes. It describes a person full to the top and sealed, which is the opposite of numbness and the opposite of complaint.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Blindness in that world ended a man's independence. He could no longer travel, judge a herd, read a face across a tent or know who had entered a room. For a patriarch it meant handing the household's practical authority to the sons whose account he did not believe. The audience would have heard the whitening of his eyes as the loss of his last means of checking anything.
studies.didYouKnow: Two of this ayah's central words occur nowhere else in the Quran: the cry of sorrow he utters and the verb describing what happened to his eyes. The Book's longest sustained portrait of grief reaches for vocabulary it never uses again, which is one reason this ayah has stayed in the memory of readers who know little else of the surah.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Grief is presented here as compatible with faith rather than as a lapse from it. A prophet weeps until he cannot see, and the surah reports it without a word of correction, then adds that he was holding it in. Endurance in this account is not the absence of pain but the containment of it, and the following ayat show where the contained thing is finally allowed to go.

crossReferences.why: Where the held sorrow is directed, once his sons object to him carrying it at all.
The sight restored, at the moment the news he has been waiting for finally arrives.
Addresses a weight that presses on the back, and places relief alongside it rather than after.

studies.applyIt: If you are holding something in, take it out once today in a form nobody else has to receive. Say it into an empty room, write it on a page you throw away, name it in a prayer. This ayah does not ask you to stop containing. It shows a man doing both, and both are in the same sentence.

studies.title: I Complain Only To God
studies.meaning: His sons object to the grieving itself, swearing he will destroy his health or die of it. His answer distinguishes two things the objection has confused. He is not complaining to them; he is pouring out what he carries to God, which is a different act with a different address. Then a second clause, harder than the first: I know from God what you do not know. Commentators read it as the hope he has never surrendered, stated plainly at the point where he looks most defeated.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Extended mourning was watched and judged in that society, and a family had views about how long was decent. No occasion is reported for these ayat. The commentators note that the sons swear an oath as they speak, using the emphatic form that recurs throughout this surah, and that their concern is real even though it is delivered as an accusation.

keyTerms.gloss: wasted, at the point of ruin
keyTerms.note: A rare word for a body worn down to the edge of collapse by grief or illness. It occurs nowhere else in the Quran, and it is what his sons think they are watching happen.
From a root meaning to scatter or disperse. It names sorrow too large to hold in one piece, laid out rather than described, and the word in this sense appears only here.
The ordinary verb for making a complaint. Its force here comes entirely from the preposition that follows: not to you, but to God, which changes the same act into something else.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Mourning had public forms and public limits. Grief was expressed loudly at the time and was expected to subside, and a man still weeping years later drew comment from his own household first. There was nowhere private to take it. What the ayah describes is a man finding an address for his sorrow that is not the people around him, in a society where everything else was said in company.
studies.didYouKnow: Both of the unusual words in these two ayat, the one for a body wasted by grief and the one for sorrow spread out, occur only here in the Quran. Within three ayat the surah uses four terms it never uses again, all of them describing what long grief does to a person, which is more specialised vocabulary than the Book spends on almost any other emotion.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Complaint is not treated as a failure of faith; its direction is what matters. The ayah separates the act of laying out sorrow from the act of protesting against God, and permits the first entirely. It also shows knowledge and grief coexisting. He says he knows something from God, and he says it while blind from weeping, so certainty here is not presented as something that removes pain.

crossReferences.why: The instruction that follows immediately: go and search, and do not despair of God's relief.
Another prophet addressing his condition to God directly rather than to the people around him.
He repeats this exact claim about knowing from God once the news finally arrives.

studies.applyIt: There is something you have stopped mentioning because people around you are tired of it. Take it somewhere else tonight rather than putting it down. Say it in full, in your own words, in prayer, without editing it into something more acceptable. The ayah's whole distinction is about who you are saying it to.

studies.title: Do Not Despair Of Relief
studies.meaning: An old man who has lost two sons sends the rest out to search, and the instruction has two halves that do not obviously belong together: go and look, and do not despair. Early scholars note the pairing, since searching is what a person does who has not given up. The word rendered as comfort is the one for a breath of relief. The sentence then defines despair by who does it, which is the sharpest thing in the verse.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, from a surah revealed during a hard stretch when little was going well for the community. By this point Jacob has lost Joseph decades earlier and Benjamin recently. He has been told his sons were involved in both. Early scholars read his instruction as the surah's centre of gravity, since everything after it moves quickly towards a reunion nobody in the story expects.

keyTerms.note: A verb built from the root for sense perception, meaning to feel your way towards information. It describes patient, active searching rather than a formal inquiry, which is why it suits a decades-old loss.
From the root that gives the words for wind and for spirit. It names relief as something arriving like moving air, and early scholars explain it as the mercy that brings ease after constriction.
The verb for abandoning expectation entirely. Its appearance twice in one verse, first as a prohibition and then as a description, turns the second occurrence into the reason for the first.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: People disappeared. Caravans were raided. Travellers died on unmarked routes. A family might wait years for news that never came. There was no authority to ask and no record to consult. Searching meant sending men to ask at wells and markets, and hoping a description was recognised. Jacob's instruction describes the only method available, and everyone listening knew how rarely it worked.
studies.didYouKnow: The word used here for God's relief is written the same as the word for spirit. It is closely related to the word for wind, and classical scholars discuss the connection. Reciters tell them apart by a vowel alone. So a listener hearing this verse hears a word for breath being used of divine mercy.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Despair is classified rather than merely discouraged, and that changes its weight. It is described as something believers do not do. So hopelessness becomes a statement about what a person takes God to be like, rather than a passing mood. The verse also refuses to separate hope from action. The same sentence sends people out to search. So trust is what keeps a search going rather than a substitute for it.

crossReferences.why: Forbids despair of God's mercy in the widest terms, addressed to everyone.
Has Abraham ask who despairs of his Lord's mercy except those who are astray.
Shows the relief arriving, carried by the shirt he had been waiting for.

studies.applyIt: Think of something you stopped hoping for and quietly stopped working on at the same time. Do one small piece of the work again this week: send the message, make the enquiry. The verse puts searching and hope in a single sentence, and the searching is the part you can actually start today.
studies.explainEasier: Jacob told his sons to go out and look for Joseph and his brother. He told them never to give up hope in God's help. Only people who do not believe give up hope like that.

studies.title: Scant Goods, And A Question
studies.meaning: They come back with almost nothing to trade and ask for two things: full measure, and charity beyond it. The word for their merchandise means goods barely worth the name, pushed along rather than carried with any confidence. Then Joseph speaks, and it is a question rather than an accusation: do you know what you did to Joseph and his brother, when you were ignorant. Commentators note the last clause. He supplies their excuse for them inside the very sentence that names the deed.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Asking for charity in a market was a public admission that a household could no longer trade its way through the season, and it cost a family standing that took years to recover. No occasion is reported for these ayat. The commentators note that the brothers are now in exactly the position they once put their father in: dependent, without leverage, and asking a stranger for mercy.

keyTerms.note: From a verb meaning to push something along that will not move easily. Applied to goods it means poor stock that a trader can hardly get accepted, and the word occurs only here in the Quran.
The verb shares a root with truthfulness, so giving is described with the vocabulary of being genuine. They are asking for more than the measure their goods can buy, which is a request for a gift.

In Quranic usage this names reckless conduct rather than lack of information. Joseph places it in his question as an available reading of what they did, before they have offered any account of themselves.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Trade in a famine year ran on whatever a family could still part with: worn goods, small quantities, things kept back for years. A merchant could refuse such stock outright. Everyone in a market knew what it meant when a party arrived with thin bundles and asked for consideration, and everyone knew the household behind them was at the end of its resources.
studies.didYouKnow: The word describing the brothers' goods occurs only here in the Quran, and it is the language of the grain market rather than of scripture. The reunion at the heart of this surah begins with a haggling term for merchandise nobody wants, spoken by men who once sold their brother for a few coins and thought him of little value.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The question Joseph asks is built to be answerable. It names the act, includes the brother they also wronged, and offers ignorance as a description of how it happened, all before they have said anything. That is a specific model of confrontation: the wrong is not minimised and the door is not closed. What follows in the next ayah depends entirely on how this sentence was framed.

crossReferences.why: The sale that this scene answers, where they set a contemptible price on him.
Their reply, and the moment recognition finally arrives after two journeys of blindness.
The full measure Joseph promised on their first visit, which they now ask for as a favour.

studies.applyIt: When you next raise something old with someone, build their way in. Name the act plainly, then add the honest mitigation you already believe: you were young, we were both exhausted, nobody explained it to you. It is not weakness in the confrontation. It is what makes an answer possible instead of a defence.

studies.title: God Has Been Gracious To Us
studies.meaning: The recognition arrives as a question and the answer is three words wide: I am Joseph, and this is my brother. Then, before anything else can be said, he moves the subject off himself. God has been gracious to us. Commentators note the plural: the favour is described as reaching all of them, brothers included, at the moment they have most reason to expect otherwise. The closing sentence gives the two conditions he attaches to what happened, mindfulness and patience, and states the reward as a rule rather than a boast.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah was heard by people who had been driven from ordinary life by relatives, and who would one day be in a position to answer that treatment. No occasion is reported for this ayah. The commentators note that the brothers' question is put with an emphatic construction, as people do when they already suspect the answer and need it said, which suggests recognition dawning rather than arriving all at once.

keyTerms.note: The verb means to bestow a favour, and its noun can also mean reproaching someone for a gift. Used of God it carries only the giving, which is why the Quran reserves this construction for divine kindness.
A plural pronoun where the sentence could have said upon me. The favour is described as landing on the whole family, including the men standing in front of him, before any of them has apologised.
Two verbs paired as a single condition: carefulness about wrongdoing and endurance under it. The surah has shown Joseph doing both, and this is the only place he names them.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Recognition after long separation was a real difficulty in that world, not a literary device. Men changed with hard years, dress and speech marked a foreign court, and the brothers had last seen a boy. There were no likenesses to compare and no way to check a claim except by what a person knew. The one thing Joseph offers as proof is a name and a relationship.
studies.didYouKnow: Joseph never states his identity as a title or an office. The self-description he gives is a name and a brother, and the sentence that follows immediately hands the credit to God. In a surah that has spent twenty ayat on his authority over Egypt's stores, the moment of revelation contains no reference to any of it.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Gratitude is used here to disarm a reckoning. By naming what happened as God's favour on all of them, Joseph removes the ground on which he could stand over his brothers, and does it before they can defend themselves or beg. The general rule he states at the end also matters: the reward is promised to a way of behaving rather than to him personally, which makes his own case an instance rather than an exception.

crossReferences.why: The same promise stated by God earlier, that the reward of those who do good is never wasted.
Their admission and his answer, where the reckoning is opened and closed in two ayat.
Joseph names the whole sequence as his Lord's subtle arrangement, once his parents arrive.

studies.applyIt: The next time you are proved right about something that hurt you, try saying the good outcome out loud without a comparison in it. No before and after, no reference to who doubted you. Just the plain fact and who you think it came from. The comparison is where most vindications go wrong, and it is easy to leave out once you notice it.

studies.title: No Blame On You Today
studies.meaning: The brothers own the wrong with no excuse. Joseph's reply is shorter than their confession. He lifts the blame, using a word for the kind of reproach that keeps being brought up again. It is not a verdict. Early scholars read the word for today in two ways. Some say it marks a limit. Others say it is there for force. Joseph then leaves the forgiving of the sin to God instead of granting it himself. He ends with the widest name for mercy.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The surah spoke to a man whose own tribe had driven him out. One day he would be in a position to answer them. Early sources record that the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) used words close to these when Mecca was taken. Scholars note the link. The surah had come down many years before that day.

keyTerms.note: A word for blame brought up again and again. Its root has to do with reproving. What Joseph drops is not the wrong itself but the constant raising of it. That is a precise thing to give up.
From a root meaning a trace or mark left behind. The brothers use it to admit the favour they had resented. Their confession names the very thing that set the whole story moving.
The strongest form of the word is set against the plural of the same word. So mercy is measured against mercy, not against anything else. The line ends the scene by pointing past the wronged man.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Making peace in tribal society was formal and costly. A wrong was settled by payment. It was settled by a public admission in front of witnesses. Often a marriage tied the two families together afterwards. Simply dropping a claim was rare, because it left the injured side with no standing. Joseph holds complete power over the men who sold him. The first listeners would have expected terms.
studies.didYouKnow: In Arabic, the confession and the reply together run shorter than the account of the crime they are about. Early scholars noticed how brief it is. They also point out what the reply leaves out. It never says what was done. It sets no conditions. It asks for nothing in return.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Forgiveness here splits into two acts, and Joseph claims only one. He drops the reproach, which was his to drop. He leaves the forgiving of the sin to God. That keeps the wronged man out of a seat he does not hold. The scene also shows a pardon given from strength, not from need. That is the only setting in which a pardon means much.

crossReferences.why: Asks whether those with means would not rather have God forgive them in turn.
Says that a pardon and making peace bring a reward from God.
Shows the father promising to ask forgiveness for them, which completes the scene.

studies.applyIt: Think of an apology you accepted while quietly keeping the event in reserve. Decide today whether the bringing up stops. That is the exact thing the word in this ayah gives up. It is a decision, not a feeling. So it is still open on a day when generous is the last thing you feel.
studies.explainEasier: Joseph's brothers finally admit they were wrong. Joseph tells them he will not hold it against them or bring it up again. He says God will forgive them, because God is the kindest of all.

studies.title: Take This Shirt Of Mine
studies.meaning: A shirt is sent back along the road a shirt once travelled. The first was carried to his father soaked in false blood; this one is to be laid on his face so that sight returns. Commentators differ over the mechanism, some treating it as a sign given to a prophet and others as an occasion at which God restored what He willed, and none of them makes the cloth itself the agent. The instruction ends with the practical part: bring me your family, all of them.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Garments carried identity in that world, and a man's shirt was recognisable to his household, which is what made the earlier deception work. No occasion is reported for this ayah. The commentators note the symmetry the surah has built without commenting on it: the object used to establish a death is used to undo the grief it caused, and the same sons carry it both times.

keyTerms.note: The word for shirt occurs six times in the Quran and every one is in this surah. It appears at each of the story's three hinges, as false evidence, as true evidence, and here as the sign of a return.
The same verb the brothers used when they agreed to cast him into the well. One word covers the disposal that began the story and the gesture that begins to close it.
Literally he will come seeing. The word for sight is the one the Quran uses for insight as well, and it returns a few ayat later when the same root describes clear knowledge of a path.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Cloth held a person's scent and shape for a long time, and a garment sent ahead of a traveller was a recognised way of announcing him. Families kept the clothes of the absent and the dead. A shirt arriving from Egypt would have been handled by everyone in the household before it reached the old man's face, and each of them would have known whose it was.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for shirt appears six times in the Quran and all six are in this surah, spread across three scenes: the bloodied shirt brought to a father, the shirt torn at the back in a locked house, and this one sent home from Egypt. One garment carries the entire plot, and the Book never mentions the item again.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage lets a physical object stand at the point where mercy arrives, without letting the object become the cause. Commentators are careful about this, and the surah is too: the shirt is laid, and the sight returns, and nothing in the wording makes the second follow from the first by itself. It also completes a pattern the story has been building. What was used to inflict the wound is what is sent to end it.

crossReferences.why: The first shirt, brought to the same father with false blood on it as proof of a death.
The shirt arrives and sight returns, along with the words he had been repeating for years.
The middle appearance of the garment, where a tear in it establishes the truth.

studies.applyIt: Think of an object connected to a hard episode in your life: a room, a piece of clothing, a route you stopped taking. Use it once this week for something ordinary and good. You are not undoing anything. You are giving the thing a second association, which is roughly what this ayah arranges.

studies.title: I Sense Joseph On The Air
studies.meaning: The caravan has only just set out and hundreds of miles away an old man says he can sense Joseph. He knows how it sounds and says so in the same breath, using a verb that means to be dismissed as senile. His household obliges immediately: you are in your old confusion. Commentators note that the surah lets the exchange stand without adjudicating it in the moment, and settles it two ayat later when the shirt arrives exactly as he has said.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and heard by people accustomed to having their convictions treated as a kind of derangement by their own relatives. No occasion is reported for these ayat. The commentators note that the sons swear an oath as they speak, and that the word they use for their father's condition is the same one they used decades earlier about his affection, so the family has kept one word for him across a lifetime.

keyTerms.note: The word means both wind and smell, so what reaches him travels on the air. Arabic keeps the two ideas in one term, and the sentence works as sensation and as intuition at the same time.
From a root about a mind weakening with age and speech losing its sense. He uses the word himself, in advance, which is the only occurrence of it in the Quran.
The same noun his sons used of him at the surah's opening, when they judged his love excessive. Adding the word for ancient turns a single judgement into a lifelong verdict.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Scent carried further than sight in that country and people trusted it. Herders smelled rain before it came, travellers knew a settlement by its smoke, and a blind man's nose and ears did the work his eyes had done. What Jacob claims would have struck the first audience as unusual in its distance rather than in its kind, which is why his sons attack his mind rather than his method.
studies.didYouKnow: The word Jacob uses when he asks his sons not to think him senile occurs only once in the Quran, here. He puts their objection into his own mouth before they can make it, and they make it anyway in the very next ayah, reaching for the same term they had used about him at the start of the story.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The surah is candid that a true perception can be indistinguishable, from outside, from an old man's decline. Nothing in the scene lets the reader tell them apart either, until the shirt arrives. That is an honest account of how knowledge from God sits in the world: it does not come with a mark on it, and the people closest to a person are often the least able to grant it.

crossReferences.why: The claim is settled two ayat later, when the shirt arrives and sight returns with it.
The same word for wandering, used by the same sons about the same father, decades earlier.
The knowledge he says he has from God, which this scene is the last test of.
