studies.applyIt: Think of the person in your family who is easiest to dismiss, and notice the phrase you use about them: they always say that, they are being dramatic. Next time they say something, hold the phrase back and ask a question instead. You may still conclude the same thing. You will have checked once.

studies.title: And He Regained His Sight
studies.meaning: The messenger is named by what he brings rather than by who he is: the bearer of good news. He lays the cloth, sight comes back, and the first thing the old man says is not about his eyes. It is the sentence he has been repeating for years, put to his sons as a question they now have to answer. Commentators note that the surah gives him no words of wonder at all. What he says is a reminder that he had said it already.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. Blindness in that world was permanent and its reversal was not something anyone expected, which is why the ayah spends its second half on speech rather than on the eyes. No occasion is reported for this ayah. The commentators note that the sons are present for the restoration, so the men who called their father confused two ayat earlier are the audience for his reply.

keyTerms.note: A person defined by the message they carry. The definite form occurs only here in the Quran, and the root is the same one the water-carrier shouted at the well when he found a boy.
The verb means to be turned back to a former state. Sight is described as restored rather than granted, which fits a man who lost it to weeping rather than to age or injury.
A rhetorical question with no gloating attached to it in the Arabic. He repeats the exact claim he made earlier, which turns a moment of vindication into a restatement rather than a rebuke.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A messenger sent ahead of a caravan rode faster than loaded animals and arrived hours or days before them. Bringing good news was a recognised role with a reward attached, and the man who carried it was welcomed at the door before anyone asked his name. That is why the ayah can call him simply the bearer of good news and expect every listener to picture the arrival exactly.
studies.didYouKnow: The root behind the word for the bearer of good news appears at both ends of this surah. It is what the water-carrier cried out at the well when his bucket came up holding a boy, and it names the man who arrives here with the shirt. The same root marks the moment Joseph is lost and the moment he is found.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Vindication is presented without triumph. He does not describe what has happened to him and does not accuse anyone; he simply says again what he had been saying, which leaves the correction to be made by the people who dismissed him. The passage also completes the surah's account of knowing from God. It was true while it looked like decline, and it is not more true now that it is visible.

crossReferences.why: The claim he is repeating here, made when he had every appearance of being wrong.
The same root for good news, shouted at the well by the man who found him.
The loss of sight this reverses, and the sorrow the surah gave as its cause.

studies.applyIt: When something you were right about finally comes out, resist the summary of who doubted you. Say the original sentence again and stop there. It gives the other person somewhere to go, and it keeps the thing you were right about at the centre rather than yourself.

studies.title: Ask Forgiveness For Our Sins
studies.meaning: Three ayat close a wound that opened ninety ayat earlier. The sons ask their father to seek forgiveness and call themselves at fault, using the word the Egyptian household once used of a woman in the wrong. His answer defers rather than refuses: I shall ask my Lord for you. Commentators discuss the delay, some connecting it to a preferred hour of prayer and others reading it simply as a promise kept later. Then the scene shifts to Egypt and a father is embraced.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and the whole passage would have been heard by people whose own families had turned on them and might one day come back. No occasion is reported for these ayat. The commentators note that the brothers ask for prayer rather than for pardon from their father directly, which fits a household in which the wrong is understood as having been done before God as well as against a man.

keyTerms.note: A request that someone else ask on their behalf. The root means to cover over, so forgiveness in this vocabulary is a fault covered rather than a fault declared not to have happened.
The particle points to a future that is not immediate. Commentators read the delay variously, and the surah leaves it unexplained, so the promise is given and its timing is not.
From the root behind faith and trust. The last word of the invitation into Egypt is the word for being safe, which is what this family has not been since the second ayah of the story.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Moving a whole household was a major undertaking: tents, herds, dependants, elderly relatives, everything a family owned walking for weeks. Such a move was made once or twice in a lifetime and only for water, land or safety. The invitation at the end of these ayat is therefore not a visit. It is the end of the family's life in one country and the beginning of another.
studies.didYouKnow: The word the brothers use of themselves here, those at fault, appeared once before in this surah, in the mouth of an Egyptian nobleman telling his wife to seek forgiveness. The same term is used of the two people in the story who wronged Joseph, and in both cases it is attached to a request for forgiveness rather than to a punishment.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Forgiveness is shown as a sequence rather than a moment. The wrong is named, the wronged party responds, an intercession is asked for and promised, and only then does the family move. The passage also keeps the final word with God. What the brothers request is not their father's pardon, which they have already received, but that someone ask on their behalf of the one they take the greater offence to have been against.

crossReferences.why: The earlier use of the same word for being at fault, in the household that imprisoned him.
Joseph's own answer to the same admission, given days earlier in Egypt.
What follows the embrace, when the dream from the fourth ayah is finally named as fulfilled.

studies.applyIt: If someone has apologised to you and you said it was fine, go back once and say something more specific: that you noticed what it cost them, or what you are letting go of. Blanket reassurance ends a conversation. A sentence with a detail in it tells the other person they were actually heard.

studies.title: My Lord Is Ever Subtle
studies.meaning: The dream from the fourth ayah is named as fulfilled, and then Joseph gives his account of what happened in between. Two things are listed as kindnesses: being brought out of prison, and his family being brought from the desert. The well, the sale and the years of slavery are not mentioned at all. The reason follows in a divine name meaning subtle and finely attentive, one who works through means too small to be noticed while they are happening.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The prostration described here belonged to the customs of that time and place as a gesture of honour before a ruler, and the commentators are unanimous that it is not worship, noting that such greeting was later set aside. No occasion is reported for this ayah. The tradition treats this as the surah's climax, where a dream given to a boy is matched to an event forty years on.

keyTerms.note: A divine name occurring seven times in the Quran. It joins gentleness with fineness, describing one whose arrangements are too delicate to be seen at work, which is exactly Joseph's point about his own life.
A verb for the small goading prod that starts a rift. Joseph uses it to describe what came between him and his brothers, naming an instigator rather than assigning the whole act to them.

keyTerms.gloss: He brought me out of prison
keyTerms.note: He names the prison and not the well. Commentators note the omission and read it as deliberate courtesy, since his brothers are standing in the room and the well was their doing.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Coming in from the open country to a settled city was a change of world. Desert life meant tents, herds and moving with the water; a city meant walls, granaries, officials and a fixed address. Arabian listeners knew both and knew that the move was rarely upward. Joseph names it as a kindness, which is how a family arriving with nothing would have experienced it.
studies.didYouKnow: In recounting his life to his father, Joseph mentions the prison and omits the well entirely, although his brothers are present and the well was their work. He also attributes the rift to an instigator rather than to them. The surah reports both omissions without comment, and neither the well nor the sale is ever raised again.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The divine name at the centre of this ayah gives the surah its final theory of itself. A God described as subtle works through the wrong turns and the delays rather than around them, and nothing in the story required a miracle to reach this room. It also shows what a person does with vindication. Joseph edits his own account to protect people who did not protect him.

crossReferences.why: The dream this ayah declares fulfilled, told by a boy who understood nothing of it.
The prayer that follows immediately, which asks for an ending rather than for more.
Uses the same divine name of subtlety, alongside provision given to whomever He wills.

studies.applyIt: Tell the story of a hard period in your life once this week, out loud, and leave out one detail that would make someone else look bad. Not to lie. Simply to notice how much of your account is load-bearing and how much is there to assign blame. Say the shorter version and see what is missing.

studies.title: Receive Me In Submission
studies.meaning: The prayer starts with a list of what was given: power, and the reading of events. Both come with a word that means some of, not all. Then Joseph names God as the one who started the heavens and the earth. The frame widens at the very moment of triumph. His two requests are not what you expect from a man at the top. He asks to die in submission. He asks to be joined to the righteous. He asks for nothing at all in this life.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. It comes at the close of the story, after the family is back together and the dream from the fourth ayah has come true. Early scholars note that the story ends with a prayer, not with the reunion. The Quran gives Joseph the last words of his own account. The surah then turns straight to the Prophet's own situation in its final ayat.

keyTerms.note: The preposition means part of. Joseph calls what he was given a portion, not rule over everything. Early scholars read this as chosen modesty, spoken at the moment he could have claimed the most.
The root means splitting something open to bring it into being. It is used of a seed breaking open, or of a first opening. Creation is named as a first tearing open, not as parts put together.
A verb for taking something in full, used of collecting a debt paid off completely. Death here is a receiving of what is owed. It is not named as an ending or as a loss.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Egypt was the grain store of the region. Its government was the most complex one the Arabian listeners knew of, though they knew it by report. A man who held the stores in a famine held everything. Meccan traders bought Egyptian grain and cloth. The size of that state was a byword. This prayer comes from the man at the top of the one system everybody agreed was mighty.
studies.didYouKnow: This is one of the very few places in the Quran where a prophet asks to die in a certain state. The request comes at his greatest worldly success, not in a hard time. Early scholars discuss that timing. They also note that he asks for company as much as for an ending.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The prayer looks back over the whole story and finds a giver behind every stage of it. That includes the stages that looked like ruin at the time. Calling God his protector in this life and the next folds the two into one bond. The requests then show what he really wants. Not the power he has just named, which he treats as a portion already handed to him. He wants a way of dying, and a company to join.

crossReferences.why: Promises him this same teaching of dreams at the very start of the story.
Records Abraham asking to be joined to the righteous in similar words.
Ends another long passage with a request to die among the truly good.

studies.applyIt: Next time something goes well, add one line to how you tell it: name what you were given rather than only what you did. Then notice what you actually want after that. Joseph's prayer at the top of his life asks for nothing in this world, and that is the part worth sitting with.
studies.explainEasier: Joseph has power in Egypt and his family is back with him. Instead of asking God for more, he thanks God for what he was given. He asks to die as a believer and to be with good people.

studies.title: You Were Not There
studies.meaning: The story stops and the surah turns to its listener. What you have just heard, it says, is news of the unseen, and the proof offered is an absence: you were not with them when they agreed on their plan. The argument turns on the well-known scene at the surah's opening, a private council among brothers with no witnesses at all. Commentators note the precision of the choice. Of every episode in the story, the one selected is the one nobody could have reported.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) was known in his own city as a man without letters or foreign learning, and the charge against him was that he had picked the material up somewhere. This ayah answers that charge by pointing at a scene no source could have supplied. No occasion is reported for it, though the surrounding passage clearly addresses the Meccan objection.

keyTerms.note: The first word means reports of consequence, the second what lies beyond perception. The phrase occurs three times in the Quran, each time introducing an account of events the listener could not have witnessed.
The same verb used in the surah's third scene, when the brothers resolved together to put a boy in a well. The ayah reaches back ninety-odd ayat and picks up the exact word.
Covert planning, close to the surah's other word for contrivance. The imperfect tense keeps them in the middle of the act, which is the moment the ayah says no human observer was present.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Knowledge in Mecca had traceable sources. A man knew what his tribe told him, what he heard at fairs, what traders brought from Syria, and what the scholars of other communities were willing to teach. Everyone could account for what anyone else knew. That is why the objection about where the material came from was the natural one, and why an ayah about absence answers it.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase for news of the unseen occurs three times in the Quran, and each occurrence closes a long narrative about people the listener never met, in each case with the same reminder that he was not present. The surahs concerned tell the stories of Mary, of Noah, and of Joseph, and the formula binds all three together.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The claim being made is narrow and checkable in principle rather than sweeping. It is not that the story is beautiful or improving but that its source cannot be human report, and it names the exact episode where that is true. The passage also shows the Quran willing to be tested. It offers a specific ground on which a listener might refuse it, rather than asking for acceptance on general grounds.

crossReferences.why: The private scene this ayah points at, where the plan was settled with nobody watching.
The same formula about news of the unseen, closing the account of Noah and his people.
The third use of the formula, after an account of Mary and those who cast lots over her.

studies.applyIt: Take one thing you believe and ask where you actually got it. Not whether it is true, only the route: who told you, and how did they know. Most of what any of us holds arrives without a receipt. Doing this once for one belief is a useful and slightly uncomfortable half hour.

studies.title: Signs They Walk Straight Past
studies.meaning: Four short ayat that let the air out of any expectation the story might have raised. Most people will not believe however much you want them to; you are asking no payment for this; the sky and the earth are full of signs people pass by without turning their heads; and most of those who do believe in God attach something else alongside Him. Commentators take the last clause as describing a mixture rather than open denial, which is the harder and more common condition.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, and addressed directly to the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) after years of preaching in a city that had largely refused him. No occasion is reported for these ayat. The commentators note that the Meccans acknowledged God as creator and supreme, and still placed intermediaries alongside Him, which is precisely the situation the fourth of these ayat describes rather than a case of outright atheism.

keyTerms.note: The verb means to want something intensely and to guard it closely. It concedes the strength of the messenger's desire and then says plainly that the desire is not what determines the outcome.
The ordinary word for payment for work. Poets, soothsayers and orators in that world were paid, so the absence of a fee removed one available explanation for why a man would say such things.
A participle picturing someone presenting their side rather than their face. It describes an averted posture rather than a stated refusal, which is what walking past a sign actually looks like.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: A man in Mecca walked under an enormous sky every night and knew the stars well enough to navigate by them. He watched wells fill, herds calve and rain turn a valley green within days. None of it was unfamiliar and all of it was ordinary, which is the point these ayat make: the signs were not being hidden from anyone, they were simply the scenery people lived in.
studies.didYouKnow: The Meccans whom these ayat address were not deniers of God. They swore by Him, named their children after Him and acknowledged Him as creator, while treating other beings as intermediaries. That is why the last of these four ayat speaks of most people believing in God while associating something with Him, rather than of people who believe in nothing.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Two things are separated here that people usually run together: the truth of a message and its reception. The passage tells a messenger that his effort is not the variable, which protects him from measuring himself by numbers. It also relocates unbelief. The problem described is not a shortage of evidence but a habit of attention, and the remedy implied is looking at what is already there.

crossReferences.why: The warning that follows immediately, addressed to people who feel entirely secure.
Addresses the same intense eagerness in a messenger and the same limit placed on it.
Names the signs in the heavens and the earth for people who take the trouble to reflect.

studies.applyIt: Go outside once this week without your phone and look up for two minutes. Not to feel anything in particular. The ayah's charge is about passing by, so the exercise is only to stop passing by, once, deliberately, and see whether two minutes is harder than it sounds.

studies.title: A Covering They Do Not Expect
studies.meaning: The question is about security rather than belief. Do they feel safe that a covering will not come over them, or that the Hour will not arrive suddenly while they are unaware. Two arrivals are named, one that falls on a people in this world and one that ends everything, and both are described as coming when nobody is braced for them. Commentators note the word for a covering, which pictures something spread over a whole population rather than aimed at individuals.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The audience knew stories of settlements on their own trade routes that had simply ended, and the Quran refers to those ruins repeatedly. No occasion is reported for this ayah. Coming immediately after a long story in which a family's situation reverses completely and without warning, the question takes its force from the ninety ayat the listener has just heard.

keyTerms.note: Built on the root behind safety and faith. The question asks about a feeling of safety rather than about a belief, which is a sharper thing to ask, since people rarely examine what makes them feel secure.
Something that comes over a thing and wraps it. The word names a whole surah elsewhere in the Quran, and here it pictures punishment as weather rather than as a blow aimed at anyone.
An adverb for arrival with no approach. The Quran uses it repeatedly of the Hour, and it rules out the assumption that anyone will get a period of notice in which to prepare.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Caravans passed abandoned settlements along the routes north and south, places whose wells still worked and whose houses stood empty. Traders told stories about them and the Quran refers to them as sites its listeners had seen with their own eyes. A people that had been secure and was suddenly not was not an abstract idea in Mecca. It was a landmark on the road to Syria.
studies.didYouKnow: The word used here for an enveloping covering gives its name to one of the short surahs near the end of the Quran, where it describes the overwhelming event itself. In this ayah it is applied to a punishment in this world, so the same term reaches across the Book from a warning inside a story to the title of a surah about the Hour.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah targets complacency rather than disbelief, and does so by asking about a feeling nobody defends because nobody notices holding it. Placing it directly after the story of Joseph is deliberate: the reader has just watched a household go from settled to ruined in a single afternoon. What the passage asks for is not fear but the removal of an assumption that tomorrow is guaranteed.

crossReferences.why: The other side of the same suddenness, where help arrives when nobody expects it either.
Puts the identical question about feeling secure, and calls that security a losing position.
Opens a surah with the same word for a covering event, applied there to the Hour itself.

studies.applyIt: Name one thing you are quietly assuming will still be there next year: your health, a relationship, an income, a parent. Not to worry about it. Just say it once, precisely, and notice that you had been counting on it without ever having decided to. Then go and do the small thing you keep postponing about it.

studies.title: This Is My Way
studies.meaning: A short statement of position, and every clause in it is doing work. The way is named as his; the activity is calling to God rather than to himself; the basis is clear sight, a word meaning evidence a person can see for themselves; and the phrase and whoever follows me extends that requirement to everyone who joins him. Commentators read the last clause as a condition rather than a courtesy: those who follow are expected to see, not merely to agree.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, spoken after years in which the message had been called poetry, sorcery and confused dreaming, and after the surah has spent a hundred ayat demonstrating what it can do. No occasion is reported for this ayah. The commentators note that it comes as an instruction to say something, which places it among the passages that give the Prophet Muhammad (peace be upon him) an exact form of words to deliver.

keyTerms.note: A road that goes somewhere, not a path in general. Naming it as his own is unusual, and the clauses that follow immediately move the destination away from him and towards God.
Insight that functions like vision: something seen rather than accepted on report. The exact phrase occurs only here in the Quran, and it sets the standard for what following is supposed to rest on.

Grammatically joined to the clause about clear sight, so the same requirement covers both. Followers are described as calling and as seeing, which makes the phrase a description of a community rather than an audience.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Following a man in that society meant attaching yourself to his fortunes: his enemies became yours, his debts touched you, and your tribe might disown you for it. People did it on the strength of kinship or of a leader's proven judgement. To make clear sight the ground of following instead was to ask for something the ordinary machinery of loyalty did not require.
studies.didYouKnow: The phrase for standing upon clear sight occurs only once in the Quran, in this ayah. It comes from the same root as the word used a dozen ayat earlier for the sight restored to an old man's eyes, so the surah moves within a few lines from physical seeing regained to insight named as the basis of a whole way of life.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The ayah defines a religious community by what its members can see rather than by whom they are attached to. That is a demanding standard and it is stated as the norm rather than as an ideal. It also fixes the direction of the invitation. What is being called for is not adherence to a person, and the clause that follows, glorifying God and disclaiming association, closes off the confusion before it can start.

crossReferences.why: The same root for sight, used a few ayat earlier of eyes that had been lost to grief.
Describes how the calling is to be done: with wisdom, good counsel, and the better argument.
Joseph makes the same declaration in prison, calling to one God and naming what the alternative is.

studies.applyIt: Take one thing you practise because it was handed to you, and spend twenty minutes this week finding out why it is done. Not to test whether you will keep it; you probably will. The exercise is to move one item from inherited to seen, which is the distinction this ayah is built around.

studies.title: Men From The Towns
studies.meaning: The answer to a demand for something more impressive is deliberately ordinary. Those sent before were men, inspired, and from the settlements rather than from the desert or from the sky. Then a challenge that requires no argument: travel and look at how it ended for the people before them. The ruins are the evidence. Commentators note that every element here refuses a marvel, and that the ayah closes by asking whether the listener will use their reason.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan. The objection this answers is recorded across the Quran: why is this man like us, why has no angel come down, why does he eat and walk in the markets. No occasion is reported for this ayah. The commentators note that the abandoned settlements referred to lay along routes Meccan traders used, so the invitation to travel and look was a practical one rather than a figure of speech.

keyTerms.note: The whole answer in four words: human beings, plural, and the revealing done to them rather than by them. The same phrasing appears twice more in the Quran, both times answering the same objection.
Settled communities rather than nomadic ones. Prophets are placed inside societies with markets, disputes and neighbours, which is where their message had to be lived rather than merely announced.
From a root meaning to follow behind. The word names what came after, and the Quran uses it repeatedly for the visible result of a people's choices, which is what a traveller can still go and see.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Meccan merchants travelled north to Syria in summer and south to Yemen in winter, and the roads passed the remains of settlements that had been prosperous and were now empty. Nobody had to be told these places existed. The ayah asks its audience to do something they already did twice a year, and to look at what they had been riding past without thinking about it.
studies.didYouKnow: The formula stating that those sent before were only men receiving revelation occurs three times in the Quran, in three different surahs, and each time it answers the same complaint about the messenger being an ordinary human being. Twice it adds the instruction to ask those who have knowledge of earlier scriptures.
studies.theologicalSignificance: Prophethood is defined here by ordinariness on purpose. A messenger who was visibly other could not be imitated, and the whole point of sending one is that his life can be followed. The passage also grounds belief in something a person can go and check, which fits the surah's method throughout. Its final question is not about faith but about whether the listener will think.

crossReferences.why: Uses the same formula about men receiving revelation, and directs questioners to those with knowledge.
Repeats it again, adding that they were not bodies that did without food.
Continues directly, describing how long those men waited before help finally reached them.

studies.applyIt: Pick one person you admire for their steadiness in something and find out one ordinary detail about how they actually manage it: what time, how often, what they gave up. Admiration at a distance is comfortable because it cannot be copied. A detail makes it a method, which is exactly what this ayah is protecting.

studies.title: Until The Messengers Despaired
studies.meaning: The sentence waits a long time before it turns. Until, when the messengers had despaired and thought they had been denied, Our help came to them. The middle clause has been read in two ways since the earliest generations, depending on how one word is vocalised: either the messengers thought their own people had made liars of them, or they feared they had been given no support. Commentators discuss both readings carefully, and either way the help arrives after the point at which hope had gone.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, near the end of a long period of rejection, addressed to a Prophet and a community who had been calling for years with little to show. No occasion is reported for this ayah. The commentators treat it as the surah's last word on waiting, coming after a story in which relief arrived only when everyone involved had stopped expecting it, and immediately before the closing statement about the whole book.

keyTerms.note: An intensified form of the verb for giving up hope. The same verb described Joseph's brothers when they despaired of persuading the governor, so the surah uses one word for both kinds of exhaustion.

The earliest generations differed over how this word is voiced, and the difference changes who is doing what. Commentators record both readings, and the tradition preserves them side by side rather than choosing.

The word covers assistance given to someone in a struggle, including vindication before onlookers. It is God's help rather than deliverance in general, and it arrives without notice at the sentence's turn.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Waiting was structural in that world. A caravan was gone for months with no word; a drought broke or did not; a message sent north might be answered in a season or never. People learned to live at the end of long silences, and they also learned what it does to a person when the silence goes on past the point where waiting still feels reasonable. This ayah is addressed to that condition.
studies.didYouKnow: This ayah preserves one of the best-known differences of vocalisation in the Quran, where a single word can be read in more than one way and the classical commentaries record the discussion at length. Both readings were current among the earliest reciters, and the tradition treats the range as part of what has been transmitted rather than as a problem to be closed.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage concedes something most religious language avoids: that people carrying a message from God can reach the end of their hope. It does not correct them for it. What it does is place the arrival of help after that point rather than before it, so despair is described as a stage in the sequence rather than a disqualification. The surah's whole story has been an argument for exactly this.

crossReferences.why: The instruction not to despair of God's relief, spoken by a man who had waited decades.
The same verb for despairing, used of the brothers when their pleading in Egypt failed.
Describes earlier believers shaken until the messenger asks when God's help will come.

studies.applyIt: If you have stopped asking for something because you no longer expect it, ask once more this week, plainly, without arguing yourself into optimism first. This ayah does not require you to feel hopeful. It describes help arriving at people who had run out, which is a different and more usable claim.

studies.title: A Lesson For Those With Minds
studies.meaning: The closing ayah names what a story is for. The word it uses means a crossing: something you pass through from one side to the other, taking the meaning across with you. Then four claims about the Book itself, arranged as a denial followed by three affirmations. Not an invented tale, but a confirmation of what came before it, a setting out of everything in detail, and guidance and mercy. Commentators note that the audience is specified: people who believe, and people with minds.
studies.historicalContext: Meccan, closing a surah that had begun by promising the finest of narrations and had then delivered a hundred and eight ayat of one continuous story. No occasion is reported for this ayah. The commentators note the charge it answers, since the Meccans said the accounts in the Quran were tales of earlier peoples, and this ayah takes that word for a fabricated story and denies it directly.

keyTerms.note: From the root for crossing a river, which also gives the word for interpreting a dream. A lesson in this vocabulary is something carried from one situation to another, not a maxim attached to the end.
The second word means the innermost part of a seed or nut, what is left when the shell is removed. It names people who get to the core of a thing rather than the merely clever.
From a root about separating things at their joints. The phrase occurs only here, and it describes a book that distinguishes and lays out rather than one that lists all information.

studies.lifeInProphetsTime: Stories were the shared property of the Arabian world and everyone knew the difference between the kinds. There were tribal boasts, tales of vanished peoples, and entertainments told at fairs that nobody was expected to believe. To close a long narrative by denying it was one of these was to place it in a category the audience had to think about, since they had listened to it as though it were the other sort.
studies.didYouKnow: The word for a lesson used here shares its root with the verb the king used when he asked his council whether any of them could interpret visions. Both mean crossing from a surface to what lies on the other side. A surah about a man who read dreams closes by asking its listener to perform the same operation on the story itself.
studies.theologicalSignificance: The passage tells the reader what to do with a narrative, which is not to admire it but to cross with it. It also sets out the Book's own claim in compact form: continuity with earlier revelation rather than replacement of it, clarification rather than mere information, and finally guidance and mercy, which are addressed to those who believe. The two conditions named, believing and understanding, are placed together.

crossReferences.why: The surah's opening promise of the finest of narrations, which this ayah closes the frame on.
Said at the start that there were signs in this family for those who ask.
Names the same people of understanding, and shows them reflecting on creation itself.

studies.applyIt: Now that the story is finished, name the one part of it that is about you. Not the moral, and not a character you admire, but the moment you recognised. Write a single sentence about it. That act of carrying something across is what the word at the centre of this ayah actually describes.
